subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister, and I do so more by way of notice than otherwise, in the absence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of the very dramatic information given by the British representatives at the fifth world power conference at Vienna to the effect that the cost of an atomic power station in relation to the power it produces is now little more than that for a modern steam station, will the government review the situation in the light of that information and consider the possibility of a plan which would make electric power from this source available to parts of Canada that are not served by hydroelectric energy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Laurent (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. gentleman has suggested, I will take this as notice. However, I can say immediately that the government will do everything possible to further the research that is now being carried out in connection with this power plant that is being established here in Canada. If we can ascertain data that will support the optimistic view that power can be produced from that energy at, as the hon. gentleman has suggested, about half of what it costs to produce power from steam otherwise, it will be a very happy development and will certainly stimulate the progress of the industrial development that is taking place

in Canada and make it easier to have it more widespread throughout the country.

subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, without in any way attempting to enter into a debate on the subject, I would point out that the statement was accompanied by the declaration that in Britain, as a result of the developments that have taken place there, they are greatly expanding their construction of atomic generated electricity plants. I would hope that with this declaration by official representatives to that effect the government will give consideration to the possibility of the application of the same considerations to our plans in this country in those areas that would be benefited.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: The government of the United Kingdom and its officials are in constant communication with our government and our officials in respect to all these projects, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that we will be very happy to take full advantage of what can be demonstrated by the work that is now being done in the United Kingdom towards the setting up of electric plants based on atomic energy.

Mr. Chairman, I make no apology for making a few remarks on this first item after listening to the Minister of Agriculture in the last five or ten minutes of his speech the last day these estimates were before the house. expenditures of his department now in relation to previous years. I just want to quote what he said as reported in Hansard of May 11 at page 3830:
The suggestion that has been made by quite a number that we should be doing something for agriculture is answered by the fact that in the last 20 years we have spent very considerably more on agriculture than was ever spent in any previous 20 years. As a matter of fact we are and have been for a considerable length of time spending ten times as much as was ever spent by any other government, either Liberal or Conservative.
Then a little bit further down the page after an interruption by the hon. member for Wentworth:
In view of the fact that we have been spending that much we are at least attempting to do something for agriculture.

When the Conservatives were in power they did not spend very much on agriculture.

Down here in the low left comer of the chart is where the farm income was when the Conservatives were in power, and ever since the Liberals have been in power it has gone constantly right up and up to the top right hand corner of the chart.
Mr. Chairman, I have here some figures in the form of a chart which I should like the consent of the house to place on Hansard. They are bureau of statistics figures; they are authentic, I can assure you; and they are the relative expenditures by the Department of Agriculture in comparison with the revenues over the last 25 years. Have I the consent of the committee to place this chart on Hansard?

Just to make a few comments before placing it on the record, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say this. With the exception of one year- and that is the year 1935,-the Conservative government in power from 1930 to 1935 spent better than two per cent of the gross revenue of the government on agriculture. In view of the circumstances during that five-year period I think that is a very good record in comparison with the record since that time. On the other hand, in 1941, which is an all time low in that 25-year period, this government only spent 1 [DOT] 5 per cent of the total national revenue of Canada on agriculture. In 1952, which was considered one of the best agricultural years we have ever had so far as revenue is concerned, this government only spent 1-6 per cent.
Now, as I said before, in the poorest year from 1930 to 1935 inclusive, the Conservative government spent 1-9 per cent. In all other cases it ranges from 2-1 per cent to 3 per cent of the total revenue. Therefore, when the minister says his government has spent more than any other government, it is not true and I hope that the members opposite will take cognizance of this fact and not be misled by the minister's assertion on that day. More than that, Mr. Chairman, these figures include the ordinary expenditures of the Department of Agriculture, the special expenditures and the war expenditures. In 1951, I want to be fair, it increased to 4 per cent but included in that 4 per cent was $92,959,000 or practically $93 million that was of a special nature. I might say that probably if the minister spent as much time on the administrative matters of his department as he does on politics he would be more conversant with the facts regarding the case.
I have a resolution dealing with the feed situation passed by the Simcoe county council and endorsed by the Brant county council which I should like to read to the house. This is a serious situation, and one which will be more serious this year than it has been in past years. The resolution reads:
Whereas because of the unfavourable seeding conditions in the spring of 1956 there is likely to be a heavy demand for western feed grains to supply Ontario farmers this fall;
And whereas the action of the wheat board in filling the bay port and lakehead elevators with export wheat and malting barley in the fall of 1955 seriously disrupted the movement of feed grains by limiting the amount of storage available;
And whereas this action on the part of the wheat board increased the cost of feed grain to Ontario farmers by making it necessary to use rail transported grain;
Be it therefore resolved that the agriculture committee of Simcoe county council respectfully request the dominion government to take any action necessary to ensure that sufficient feed grain is stored in bay port elevators before the

close of navigation in the fall of 1956 to adequately supply the requirements of Ontario farmers until the opening of navigation in 1957.
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, anyone who has travelled anywhere in eastern Canada in the last two months must realize the seriousness of this situation, where field after field of spring grain was flooded out, the fields worked up again and sown to other crops. I hope the government does recognize this fact and take suitable action.
Now, I am sure that the turkey growers of Canada would want me to say that they appreciate the action the government finally took after many long years in changing the tariff regulations in order to protect the turkey growers of this country. It was long overdue. They would wish me to show their appreciation of the government for finally taking this action.
There are two other things, Mr. Chairman, that have not been acted upon as yet. It follows upon sessional paper 141-H, dated May 15, and has to do with grading regulations and packaging regulations affecting turkeys coming into Canada. According to the answer I received, grading regulations affecting turkeys imported into Canada are the Canadian regulations and they must adhere to those regulations. I am informed by reliable sources that in all cases that is not the fact. Imported turkeys are sold in Canada under grade; that is, the grades do not conform with our Canadian grades standard and there is some laxity in checking those turkeys as they cross the border to make sure that they are up to the Canadian grades standard. I hope the government will check on this matter and see that they do conform to the Canadian grades.
With regard to packaging, packaging comes under the Food and Drugs Act. I am told by reliable sources that on some of those turkeys imported into Canada there is a cellophane bag that practically covers the whole breast of the turkey, with colouring on the outside of the bag. As I understand it, that is against Canadian regulations. I have not seen one of those turkeys myself, but I am reliably informed that was the case last year. I hope the government will take suitable steps to stop this practice.
In his speech on May 11, as recorded at page 3819 of Hansard, the minister brought to our attention a project to sell milk in schools. I would like the minister to state further actually what that project was and whether it has been brought to the attention of the provinces, and whether the plan would be taken to the provinces instead of waiting for the provinces to suggest it to the government. If the provinces knew that such a project was to be undertaken by the federal

Supply-Agriculture
government, I am sure that many of them would take up the suggestion and act upon it.
Another matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the government has to do with the setup of the Department of Agriculture. Several years ago the Canadian veterinary medical association sent a resolution to the minister regarding the setup of the production service. I know the minister is aware of this fact. The resolution was brought to his attention in 1949. Something has been done since in the way of moving the animal pathology and research division from the science service to production service. That is a step in the right direction and is appreciated by the association, but their request went farther than that. Their request was that the animal pathology and research division and the health of animals division be placed in one separate branch under the direction of a veterinarian. This in no way has anything to do with the personnel of the branch; it is in no way critical of the personnel. I do not want to be misrepresented as suggesting that. They have had very good co-operation from the director of the production service. They appreciate what was done, but the feeling among veterinarians across Canada and among members of the association across Canada is that the veterinarians in the government service could do a better job for Canada if this were under one branch of the department. I think the minister will agree with me on that. The fact that there are many in the department who are members of the organization to which I refer does add force to this resolution that they ask be given consideration.
I believe since 1949 the minister has had several letters. I understand that there was a period when it was not desirable to do this and the minister knows about it, but I think the situation has resolved itself. If the minister would give consideration to this it would be appreciated by the Canadian association.

Generally speaking, this research is carried on in the parts of universities associated with agricultural activity. Some universities have agricultural colleges on their campuses. This is true of universities in western Canada. The work being carried on by way of research is aided under this vote.

The list here shows the University of Ottawa, Ottawa; Ontario Agricultural College, Guelph-even though it has that separate campus at Guelph it is still done through this school-the school at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, Quebec; University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon; University of Manitoba, Winnipeg; University of Alberta, Edmonton; University of Saskatchewan; University of Manitoba; Ontario Agricultural College; Macdonald College; University of Alberta; University of British Columbia; University of New Brunswick, Fredericton; University of British Columbia, Vancouver; McGill University, Montreal; University of Alberta; McGill University; University of Saskatchewan; Macdonald College; Hamilton College, McMaster University, Hamilton; University of British Columbia, Vancouver; University of British Columbia.
That list does not include the science service laboratory at Western university, London. Does that come under a separate item?
We operate that one directly.

Is any
progress being made in developing a variety of wheat which is rust resistant? It will be remembered that two years ago our wheat, particularly in Alberta, was practically ruined by rust.

Work is being carried on all the time at the laboratory in Winnipeg and efforts are being made to keep ahead of rust attacks. There is an improved variety of Selkirk which is not yet ready for distribution.

How
soon may we expect this new variety of Selkirk wheat to be available for seed purposes?

It is still in the testing stage and it will take two or three years to bring it to the point where it can be distributed. As all hon. members from the west know, there must be a multiplication period after it has been determined that a variety is resistant. That is handled by sending seed to California to double the speed in getting quantities available for distribution, but will take two or three years after the tests are complete.
Is any progress being made in finding a rust-resistant sunflower? The minister will remember that there was considerable damage to the sunflower industry in Manitoba through rust.
A rust-resistant sunflower has been developed and is being utilized in the Morden area of Manitoba.
What studies are being carried on at the science service laboratory at Western University?
Studies are being made of the utilization of new chemicals in the development of plant life. That is the main investigation being carried on.

6.	Bacteriology, $242,748.
What research is being carried on in relation to butter held in storage and how much butter in storage has been down-graded upon leaving storage?

I have not the exact figure of the amount that has been graded down, but it is less than 5 per cent. Of course, the grading is done by our professional graders, who grade the butter in and grade it out of plants. They use the same practice in grading it out as they use in grading it in. All the tests that are made to determine whether or not the butter is grade A1 are used in both cases.	[DOT]
Supply-Agriculture
What happens to the butter that is graded down and that does not come up to the grade A standard?

Whatever is sold out is sold at whatever grades it is graded to. The only butter of which we take delivery under the plan is grade 1. Then, when anyone purchases butter, it is delivered as grade 1. But, if there is grade 2 butter there or if there is butter that is not fit for human consumption, it is sold just as what it is.

I hope that butter of grade 2 or lower does not find itself in the retail market to be sold as butter, because there is nothing that would destroy the butter market quicker than to have the low grade butter placed in stores and sold. I hope that matter is very closely watched and dealt with by the government, because it could be very serious.
I understand the grade 2 butter is only sold by the board to manufacturers who utilize it in making candy and things like that.

How long does the butter stay at grade 1 after it has been sold? I am thinking of some experiences a client of mine had who bought grade 1 butter from storage in one province and had it sent to a plant in Nova Scotia. When it arrived there and was graded it was found to be substantially below grade 1. There was a question as to how long it had been in storage and as to what adjustment might be made by the board. What is the procedure with respect to that?

I have no information with regard to that case, of course, but it is very difficult to determine just how long butter is held after it is purchased. I think I said here once before, after making inquiries, that it will keep at least as long as a year and a half if it has been properly made in the first place. There might be mistakes in grading when it comes in which result in butter going bad, or there might be conditions in the storage that result in its going bad, but, as has already been said, the full quantity is less than 5 per cent over the period in which we have been handling it. So not very much of it has gone bad.

What does the board do as far as adjustments are concerned in such cases when butter has been sold as grade 1 and the inspector refuses to take it? Have you had any difficulty in getting adjustments from the vendor of that butter?

The responsibility there is on the person who purchased the butter and held it in the meantime. If it is ten days

Supply-Agriculture
later, something may have happened to it. We do not take responsibility for that.

In the case I was speaking of, you did not hold it at all; it was bought and delivered, and before it was taken out of the car the departmental inspector inspected it and refused to pass it at the grade at which it had been bought in another province. He did not take delivery of it.

It depends on whether he bought it directly from us or from a dealer. If he bought it from a dealer and it was butter that had been in storage before, it would be a matter between him and the dealer. If he got it directly from us, I presume that until it was delivered it was not his butter and he would then get it at whatever it graded.

If the minister is considering any changes next year in the arrangements about the subsidized butter that goes to the charitable institutions, I might say I have had very warm letters of approval of the government's policy in that regard and I certainly hope the arrangements are continued, notwithstanding the apparent lack of success in convincing the governments in some of the provinces that they should quit using margarine and use the subsidized butter.

I should like to correct an impression that might have gone out as a result of the statement I made some time ago before all the information was available, to the effect that the increase in consumption had not been high but had been comparatively low. I have some doubts as to whether that is a correct indication of what happened. The annual report which is now being prepared indicates that there was an increase of about 9 per cent in the amount of butter consumed under this plan, which some people might consider to be worth while. I may say I have had similar letters from institutions indicating that they were very much concerned that the plan should be continued, and up until now it is being continued.

I wonder whether the minister would tell us this. When the butter is purchased from the trade and taken off the market, where is it stored? Is it stored in a government warehouse or in various places around the country in the trade's warehouses?

The greater part of it remains stored right where it is when the butter comes from the market. We have a standing offer of 58 cents. If the butter comes to us because no one else will buy it at 58 cents, then it is put into storage that
rMr. Gardiner.]
is satisfactory to us. We have no storage in which to put it. Sometimes, when we realize that the butter will be utilized in some other part of Canada than where it was produced, we may ask to have it stored in that other part of Canada.

Is it marked in any way
by the department's inspectors when it is taken over?
It is all branded with the date of manufacture, the plant that manufactured it and so on, but the butter is held by the government.
It is rather late this year, minister whether boys' and girls' camps throughout the dominion qualify to receive the butter at the lower price.
I am not certain whether they would qualify but I understand they have not purchased any butter under the plan.

I should like to ask the
minister a supplementary question. What is the minimum amount of butter that the board will issue under that plan?

We have not set a minimum. We have simply set the type of institution to which we will sell the butter at the low rate, and I presume that the institutions using the butter buy all their butter from us at that rate rather than pay the extra 20 cents. I should say that they buy it from the regular supplier. We are notified as to the amount and we make the payments to the dealer.

It is rather late this year, but if the plan is carried on for another year would the minister consider allowing boys' and girls' camps across the dominion to avail themselves of the opportunity of obtaining that butter?

There is no doubt that if they made application it would be considered. I am not in a position to state whether or not it would be agreed that that is the kind of institution that it is intended should be covered.
Would the minister tell us what portion of this money under item 6 is being spent in the four western provinces?
That is item No. 6?
Yes.
I understand there is very little of it being spent. Most of it is being spent here in Ottawa.
Could the minister outline to the committee the general branches of bacteriology which are being studied?

The activities of the division may be divided into three categories, namely, research, direct service, and regulatory control work. Research, the chief function of the division, is carried on chiefly in co-operation with the experimental farm service and other divisions of science service along the following lines: Dairy bacteriology, food microbiology, soil microbiology, general microbiology. Direct service involves the analysis of samples, legume seed inoculants and control of central experimental farm diary operation. The regulatory control work is concerned with official quality control of various products coming within the scope of acts and regulations administered by the Department of Agriculture and to note conformity with standards. The products included are legume inoculants, edible gelatine, canned tomato products, frozen and dehydrated vegetables and fruits, powdered and frozen eggs, pasteurized honey and powdered milk.

I should like to support the request made by the member for Vancouver South in connection with the policy of selling butter to institutions. I have received various representations from institutions in my county which are very anxious to hear from the minister and the government that this policy will be continued.

Item agreed to.
7.	Botany and plant pathology, $1,474,719.

Can the minister tell me whether anything new has been discovered to stop loose smut in wheat? The old method was pretty cumbersome and I understand there have been some changes and that there are some new fungicides. What is the latest development in that regard?

The old treatment, of course, was the bluestone treatment which was quite general, but control of smuts of the cereal grains can be done by seed treatment. The hot water treatment is the only one that will control the loose smuts of wheat and barley, but on account of the special equipment required for this treatment and the necessity of controlling the water temperature accurately the application of the treatment is restricted to relatively small lots of high quality seed intended for increase.
A recent development that has taken place, as yet on a small scale, in both eastern and western Canada is the provision in certain localities of special equipment for treating farmers' seed with hot water. The plant pathological laboratory at Edmonton has experimented with considerable success with a simplified chemical treatment and a cold water soap treatment for the control of loose
Supply-Agriculture
smut of barley. The Saskatoon laboratory has recently developed an embryo test to detect smut of barley that promises to give more reliable results than the present method of field inspection.
Then there is formaldehyde, which is a treatment that has been used for a long period. The treatment continued to be the common treatment for the control of bunt of wheat, loose and covered smuts of oats and covered and false loose smut of barley. When properly applied it is effective but it has the disadvantage that it frequently results in seed injury. Recent advances in seed treatment materials have resulted in the general use of organic mercury compounds applied to the seed as a dust, a liquid or in a concentrated paste usually referred to as a slurry. The organic mercury compounds used for seed treatment in Canada are Ceresan dust, Lay-tosan dust, Ceresan M applied as a slurry and Panogen applied as a liquid. I find as much difficulty with these terms as the Minister of Trade and Commerce did with his.
Is there not another one, Spergon, used for loose smut? I understand they are using a very low concentration and soaking it in water at room temperature.
They are experimenting with a lot of others, including Spergon, and I do not know when the department will be prepared to make a recommendation.
You have no definite recommendation on that one yet?
No, I understand not.

As the minister knows, item 7 deals with one phase of our agricultural economy which is of great interest in the apple industry, the pathological studies that are made in that regard. I was wondering just what the breakdown of this item would be. Actually the experimental farm at Kent-ville has been specializing largely in the last few years and under the recent management in dealing with problems of pathology, botany and fungicides, everything that has to do with the apple industry, rather than operating as a general experimental farm, although it does have some livestock and some poultry. Is there a separate allocation under this item? Can the minister tell us how much of the study of botany and plant pathology at the experimental farm at Kent-ville is done under this item or is it included in the experimental farm service votes? If it is a separate item, I should like the minister to give us a breakdown and indicate how much of the vote of $1,474,000 is to be spent on the work in the Annapolis valley having to do with the fruit industry of Nova Scotia?

Supply-Agriculture
It is not easily available Mr. Gardiner: No. I understand the variety but we will get that and bring it back after has not yet been uncovered that will permit lunch.	that distribution.
I suspect a lot of it may be in the experimental farms vote.
I think probably it is but there is an amount under this item which is spent there.
Will the minister check on that?
Yes.

Can the minister say whether any work is being done to develop a suitable type of barley for export to Japan? I understand there is quite a possibility of expanding our sales of barley to that country but that they prefer a white barley.

Yes. There are three different places where experiments are being carried on, one at Lethbridge, one at Lacombe and one at Winnipeg. No particular variety has yet been announced as being particularly suitable for that but work is being done on it.

Just on that point may I say that I am hopeful that the department will expedite the breeding to which the minister has referred. Since there has been a tremendous falling off in the Japanese market for Canadian barley, because we have been informed that the Japanese prefer a barley with the white hull rather than the barley that we have in quantity with a brown or green hull, I am wondering whether the minister can say whether there is any hope for the early release of a variety that will give us some hope of getting back into what in very recent years has been an extremely important market for Canadian barley?

The effort, of course, is
being made to get that matter dealt with as soon as possible. I understand it is the weathering effect upon the barley which creates the colour which they do not wish to have. An effort is being made to overcome that difficulty. I cannot say how soon they will be successful in doing it, but they are working diligently on the problem.

As I understand it, it is the
end product, after the cooking process, with which we are concerned. The Japanese like barley that, after it is cooked, turns out as near the colour of rice as possible. Can the minister say whether a variety, even in the small quantities with which the breeders have to deal, has yet been discovered, or is only the breeding process itself still going on, or are they to the point of multiplying a variety that has some promise?

Along that
same line, may I ask this question? Would it not be possible to import some foundation stock that would be suitable so that too much time would not be lost?
We have imported varieties from Australia and from wherever we feel there is any variety that might be developed suitably. However, up to now we have not been able to recommend any particular one.

I understand
that most of the research work in weed control is closely allied with the botany division in discovering the life cycles or growing cycles of weeds. I am wondering whether in the department any recent developments have taken place which would indicate that controls for such extremely bad weeds as toad flax are appearing and what activities the department is undertaking in order to control this weed. Further, I should like to know whether the work, with the co-operation which the department has had from entomology, in developing a selected parasite to control toad flax is proceeding at as rapid a pace as is hoped?
I understand that it is proceeding as rapidly as can be expected under the circumstances. Every effort is being made to improve upon what is already being done.

While we are on the question of weeds, may I say that one of the worst ones with which we are plagued on heavy land is wild oats. I know that many farmers "sowed wild oats" in their younger days; but since then they have been having a great deal of trouble in eradicating them from their land. I was wondering whether the minister could tell us about any procedure for eradicating them. I understand that there is a form of spray that can be used on wild oats, but it seems to be very hard to spray wild oats without killing the other types of grains.

There is being developed a chemical spray which it is hoped will deal with wild oats. But so far as we know up to the present time there is only one way to deal with wild oats and that is by good farming. The chief way of successfully treating wild oats out in the west that I know of is in the sowing of rye. Rye sown by August 10 on summer fallow will get rid of wild oats in just one round. I know that. Hon. members may shake heads all they like. I farm out there. Most of the people who farm

out west sow their fall rye on stubble. But if one wants to get rid of wild oats, one can get rid of four crops in one year by summer fallowing to August 10; by sowing your fall rye on August 10 thus getting two crops of wild oats and that way you get two more crops before you take the rye off. Four crops in fall and spring will clean them out. If anyone has not tried it, he had better do so. It is more successful than any spray yet found.
As the minister knows, the viability of a wild oat seed will persist up to fifty years.
It will if you do not sprout it. But if you farm so as to sprout it, four crops will clean your land.

Just to get off this wild oats question for a moment may I ask a question about another matter. From studying the minister's report I notice that at page 53 they mention the increased use of newer herbicides for weed control, and they mention the use of these herbicides to control quack grass, buckwheat, wild oats and so on. However, I have not yet been able to find any information at all as to whether investigations are being carried on to control the spread of toadflax in western Alberta. If that information is available, I should certainly like to get my hands on it. I know that in my part of the province of Alberta the toadflax menace is rapidly growing. There is acre after acre of land that is now of absolutely no use at all.

I should like to agree with the Minister of Agriculture with regard to wild oats. Any person who knows anything about farming knows that you do not have to put up with wild oats for very long if you farm properly. If farmers are careless or negligent, they will grow wild oats.

Mr. Chairman, I believe considerable work has been done in developing rust-resistant varieties of Durum wheat that would be suitable for the market. As the minister knows, better varieties of Durum wheat are at present relatively susceptible to rust, and the whole Manitoba area and the area of eastern Saskatchewan which normally grow a great deal of Durum wheat, to a large extent have been obliged to abandon that crop because of the rust menace. The growing of Durum wheat has moved to western Saskatchewan and Alberta to a considerable extent. I wonder whether the minister can describe to us some of the work in that regard and tell us when some of these new varieties may be released in quantity.

There are two varieties of rust-resistant Durum wheat which have been
Supply-Agriculture
imported from North Dakota, and we are multiplying those now for distribution. Just as soon as they are multiplied sufficiently they will be distributed in the west. The work is at the seed-growing stage now. Some of the seed is out among the seed growers who are multiplying it.

8.	Chemistry, $754,679.

I wonder whether the minister can say what research has been done in regard to the chemical control of wheat that is infested with red mites. The farmers have continued to be warned to check their wheat in order to see whether their wheat is infested or not. Then the recommendation is made that if it is infested the wheat should be turned from one bin to another. When the bins are all full of wheat, it is not always easy to change wheat over from one bin to another. I have seen advertisements recommending certain kinds of chemicals that can be used to treat wheat whilst it is still in the bin. In addition, warnings have been issued that if these chemicals are used, the wheat may be affected in such a way that it will not be suitable for human consumption. I was wondering whether the minister can say whether or not there is any safe treatment for wheat that has become infested.

We have no information here on that, but I know what my hon. friend is speaking about. He refers to the mites that get in bins. We have been accustomed to saying that they get into the spots where the pipe has been running grain into the bin, the dust gathers there and mites form and destroy the grain in the bin. We will have that information looked up.
I know of one farmer who used gas to destroy the mites and afterwards the wheat was condemned as not being suitable, so apparently one has to be careful about the treatment one uses.
