9.	Entomology, Including a grant of $40,000 to the international congress of entomology to assist in defraying the cost of the tenth international congress of entomology to be held in Canada in 1956, $2,210,475.

Has the minister or his department had any word from southwestern Ontario as to the possibility of an infestation of army worms this season? The reason I ask that question is that there were two different representations while I was home last week end that there were quite a number of them showing up in some fields. When the minister is replying, has he any

Supply-Agriculture
information on materials being readily available in case the infestation should become worse?

The army worm which was so widespread and caused serious loss in 1954 occurred in only a few very local areas in 1955. Practically no losses occurred in those areas and the army worm disappeared early in the season. Now, that is the only record which we have of them. I did not hear that there was any serious infestation in Ontario. Of course, that is looked after primarily by the provincial agricultural authorities, but as the army worms do not pay any attention to boundary lines we do try to keep records and assist in every way possible, but most of that kind of work is done by the provincial people.
What is the latest information you have on the best method of control?
I am sorry, but the official who is in charge of that is not here at the moment. I shall get him and have this information available later.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I notice that in this item there is a reference to the tenth international congress on entomology to be held in Canada in 1956. I wonder if the minister could inform the house where that is going to be held and when?
It is to be held in Montreal in August. The delegates will visit the Ottawa farm here and make an excursion into other parts of Canada.
My hon. friend has just asked the question I was going to ask, Mr. Chairman.

In connection with this infestation of army worms, I wonder what has been the result of the experiment in the northern United States whereby they drop horseflies out of aircraft. As a matter of fact, I saw this done last year in Wisconsin, and I am just wondering if there is any information available or if consideration of this proposition has been given?

I do not know whether I was listening carefully enough, but I thought my hon. friend said it was horseflies they were dropping. I understand it is an insect which resembles the horsefly but it is not the horsefly. The treatment is the same as that used in connection with the cutworm. A little insect is distributed in considerable numbers and it goes around stinging the cutworm. It lays an egg in the cutworm which develops

into another little worm which eats the cutworm. The plan is the same in connection with the army worm, but it is a different insect that is utilized.

It is quite an amusing thing, but as a matter of fact everyone called them horseflies and the minister's explanation seems to cover it. There is one other thing I should like to ask the minister. Certain mites or other similar animals have been causing a great deal of concern in northern Saskatchewan in connection with some types of clothing. A United States flying service came into that part of the country and brought in lady bugs. They had a specially equipped plane and exhausted these lady bugs out of the plane. This had a good effect, and I am wondering if there has been any experimentation along that line?

I do not know the history of lady bugs or that kind of thing. For many years we have been not only conducting experiments but doing work in assisting in the distribution of parasites. This matter has been discussed I think in almost every session during the 20 years I have been here. We have had considerable success in breeding these insects and seeing that they are distributed.
The reason I mentioned the cutworm in particular is that I have watched the results of the experiments conducted on the prairies. It has often been said that the cutworm is difficult to destroy as long as the field remains dry. The cutworm works underground and when it rains it has to come up on top in order to get air. If you go over a summer fallow field or a wheat field that is infested with cutworms, you will find that after a rain the soil is broken and the worm has come up on top. It is then that the parasite gets busy and goes around stinging these cutworms, killing them by thousands. The breeding of these parasites is carried on by the department and we distribute them. They fly about killing cutworms, army worms and different parasites that infest our crops.

On that same point, I wish the minister would use his influence to ensure, the continuation of an experiment which was carried on in connection with the control of toadflax. The entomology department discovered a species of beetle, which was bred for the purpose of destroying the toadflax they had in Ontario. They took this same beetle to western Canada and found it was selective enough in its diet that it only ate the toadflax. Unfortunately, the experiment stopped there, and I think it is very important that they continue the experiment in the control

of toadflax. I think it is a very important trend in the control of toadflax and I wish the authorities would ensure the continuation of the experiment because it might have very beneficial consequences.
I understand the work is still going on. There is a little difficulty in getting sufficient numbers of the insect in order to have them multiply as fast as we require.

Has the minister any knowledge of the fly, bug, or whatever it is, called the heel fly, that is infesting cattle? We have a great deal of trouble in our county. They just drive a bunch of cattle almost crazy.

We have been carrying on activities in connection with that at Lethbridge particularly. It is what is known as the warble fly, I think, that stings cattle. Sprays have been used in connection with them. We are now carrying on activities on the Guelph farm in Ontario.

I should like to touch on the question brought up by the hon. member for Middlesex East in connection with army worms. The time may arrive when the infestation will be a calamity to farmers. Have any plans been laid down by the department, in conjunction with the provincial governments, to combat this pest? What makes me ask the question is that a couple of years ago in some instances in Bruce the infestation of army worms was getting very alarming. I had occasion to wire the ministers of agriculture of Ontario and of Canada. The reply I received from the federal Minister of Agriculture was that it was strictly a provincial responsibility. I understand that at times spraying and dusting has been done to good advantage in connection with army worms. I should like to have some information. If this infestation should reach such a stage-and I hope it never will-that it becomes alarming, have any plans been made in connection with getting machines to do the dusting and spraying, or has anything been done along that line?

As the hon. member said, Mr. Chairman, the present position is, and has been over the years, that that kind of Work is carried on by the provincial departments. They have been flighting grasshoppers in the west and it is the provincial departments that put on that program. In the other provinces, when any difficulty of that kind arises, it is the provincial governments that carry on. The authorities in the provincial departments come to Ottawa for advice on
Supply-Agriculture
the technical sides of it, and on any knowledge that we have on the methods that are used in other countries or in other places. We gather all the information that we can on these kinds of things through these bureaux that are established here and there and that we support. We give them all the information we can. Then, too, on the matter of the movement, that is, the movement of grasshoppers, which is a little different from the other insects, but nevertheless they do move across the country. When a movement of that kind starts down in the United States and moves toward Canada we keep the provincial authorities informed as much as we can on what we know of it; but the actual putting on of a program in order to combat it within a province is carried on by the provincial governments.

Does the federal government take any interest in the matter or pay anything toward the work that is done in connection with dusting and spraying, or is that done strictly by the provincial governments or by the companies?
We do cover some of the costs in connection with research. As a matter of fact, we carry on the work but in the actual battling of it the work is done and financed by the provinces.

While we are discussing worms and bugs I should like to refer to the situation that existed in British Columbia last year with reference to the corn ear worm. I brought to the attention of the minister and the department the fact that corn infected with corn ear worm was being imported from the United States, and growers in British Columbia were afraid that it would become an established problem as far as their crops were concerned. If I remember the correspondence aright, I was advised that corn ear worm had already established itself in the crops in British Columbia and I was wondering just to what extent that is so? What information has the department on that particular matter?

Well, the only information we have is that it has been investigated in British Columbia and been established that the worm has been there for some time. It is not just being imported now in corn that is being brought in. Apparently, it has been up and down the coast.
Is it established to any great extent or is it on a comparatively small scale?

Well, I understand it is comparatively small because, as you know, British Columbia is not a large producer of corn.

Supply-Agriculture
They grow garden corn and other kinds of corn. It is more prevalent in the states to the south than it is in British Columbia.

Will the minister and the department keep a check on it this year?
I am speaking now with reference to the importation of such corn. Will the department see that nothing further in that line is imported into the country?

Well, we shall certainly keep a check on it. I am not too certain as to whether we have all the authority that is necessary in order to prevent somebody in British Columbia from buying it across the line in the state of Washington and bringing it in. We might have difficulties, but nevertheless we do keep a check on it and try to prevent the spread of it.

Mr. Chairman, last spring there was a serious outbreak of scrapies in some of the sheep flocks in western Canada. At that time it was reported that the federal veterinarians were taking brain samples and blood samples of those sheep in order to get a better idea of the cause of this disease. Has the minister any report to make to the committee in connection with any findings that have resulted from the investigations made?
I can give only general statements with regard to it at the moment. I wonder whether my hon. friend would leave it until we reach item No. 20?

I had
thought of doing that, Mr. Chairman, but it has to do with the science service.
No; it has to do with health of animals.

Item agreed to.
10.	Forest biology, $2,167,733.

I imagine this is one of the newer items within the lifetime and experience of the minister because it is growing every year. There was a time, I presume, when forest biology as such was a very minor matter so far as the federal Department of Agriculture was concerned. Today, and quite properly so, it is becoming more and more important as time goes on. I presume this work is now done in co-operation largely with the provinces, but certain scientific work is done in the minister's own laboratories. For instance, the province of New Brunswick conducted an extensive spraying operation in connection with budworm, I think it was. Is there some basis of co-operation between the two governments under which that is done? Incidentally, there have been reports, as the ministers knows, of bitter criticism
	1 w ill'!'
from either pseudo or genuine fishermen who say that as a result of the spraying operations a great deal of damage has been done to the fish; that the spray is so efficient it not only kills the infestation on the trees but it also kills everything living in the waters, the brooks and the streams which run through the woods. I wonder if the minister has any comment to make on that and if he can indicate if there is any way in which this can be dealt with.
I also have a local problem to present to the minister which I presume would come under this item. A blight of some kind seems to be attacking birch trees in Nova Scotia and many of them appear burned as though from a forest fire. This is a recent occurrence in this area and I wonder if the department is co-operating with the province in that particular matter and, if so, what is being done about it? Would the minister give a general breakdown and what the distribution has been among the provinces?

As the hon. member has stated, this is something which has been going on for some considerable length of time, that is co-operation between the forestry branch of the department and the forestry branches of the provincial governments. The interest of the Department of Agriculture is associated with the fact that in this country we do not include forestry with our agriculture, as is the case in most countries where the growing of trees and the planting of trees on land is considered to be agriculture just as is the growing of wheat on land. It may be that, because our country was practically covered with forest to begin with and that natural resources are under the provinces, it was decided that they should carry on most of the work having to do with forestry.
The fact that we make a study of insects and all that kind of thing and the fact that we have the facilities to do a considerable part of the work which forestry branches might require to have done has indicated the need for co-operation between the forestry branches of the provinces and the branch of our department. Our branch produces different parasites in connection with the fighting of plant diseases and also studies diseases that attack trees such as the one just referred to. There is very close co-operation between the provinces and this branch of the department.
I have here an outline of the work which has been done in connection with the die-back of birch and the bronze birch borer. Heavy mortality of birch occurred in the maritime provinces and eastern Quebec in the period 1935-1947. Intensive studies showed that no

single biological agent is primarily responsible for the disease; however, the bronze birch borer is almost invariably found in deteriorating trees and may be a contributory factor in their ultimate death. More recent studies of birch rootlets and mycorrhiza have indicated that these structures are sensitive to minor changes in soil temperature and moisture. Weather records indicate the prevalence of higher than normal temperature and reduced average precipitation during the period when trees were dying. Permanent sample plots have been established in western Quebec and Ontario to determine whether similar injury may occur in these areas.
Since 1947, definite recovery of surviving trees has been evident in the maritime provinces and eastern Quebec.
Detailed root-washing experiments have been undertaken in New Brunswick and Ontario. In trees showing recovery most of the rootlets were alive with an abundance of mycorrhiza. In the years when die-back was severe, affected trees had a higher percentage of their rootlets dead with a complete absence of associated mycorrhiza. It is possible, therefore, that the dying of tops of trees was preceded by an abnormal condition within the root system which may have arisen as the result of some unfavourable environmental factor.
Root-washing experiments will be continued to determine the rootlet and mycor-rhizal conditions in birch trees. Controlled experiments on the temperature relationships of birch rootlets and the associated mycorrhiza will be continued. Ecological studies of birch in Quebec and Ontario will be continued. Studies of virus diseases of birch will be continued in the maritime provinces.
I might say in relation to that that over the radio this morning I heard someone explaining why some of the cedar hedges out at the farm are damaged.

I think everyone appreciates the seriousness of the situation with regard to the spruce budworm. Last year I asked the minister if anything was being done about the pine shoot moth which had appeared in southwestern Ontario. I see by the item that there has been an increase of 47 in the staff of the forest biological division and an increase of some $200,000 in the vote. I think we will all agree that this is very important work.
What has been the result of the experimental work in connection with the spruce budworm apart from the killing of fish, or at least most of them, and also what have been the results in connection with the pine shoot moth? I understand that the only things
Supply-Agriculture
that will kill this are certain sprays and that cold weather will destroy them as effectively as anything else.

The position with regard to the spruce budworm is this. In 1955, spruce budworm infestations again caused heavy defoliation in northern New Brunswick and in the Gaspe peninsula. Some tree mortality occurred in 1954 and 1955, in unsprayed areas and in others sprayed too late to be effective. In Ontario, heavy infestations persisted on Sibley peninsula and Black Bay peninsula, as well as between Lake Seul, Minnesota, and the Manitoba border, with extensions into eastern Manitoba. There was little change from 1954 in the infestation at Namew lake on the Manitoba-Saskatchewan border. Moderate to heavy infestations occurred in white spruce stands along the Mackenzie river for about 400 miles north of Fort Simpson in the Northwest Territories. In British Columbia, the infestations in the Harrison-lake-Lillooet river section of the lower Fraser drainage showed some enlargement, but a reduction in intensity.
The investigations carried out in New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia during recent years have yielded much information on the life history, habits, ecology, natural control, and epidemiology of the spruce budworm. A considerable proportion of the information has been published in scientific, professional and trade journals.
Studies of the effects of aerial sprays of DDT on budworm populations were continued in New Brunswick and in the Gaspe peninsula. The forest biology division worked closely with the provincial authorities and the forest industry in defining areas in which chemical control operations were required, assisted in some of the technical aspects of the spraying operations, and carried out biological studies and population counts in sprayed areas as well as in check areas reserved from spraying operations. Reports on the results of the spraying operations have been distributed.
(c) Work contemplated for 1956-57. The program of basic studies of the budworm problem will be continued in New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, and Alberta. Infestations not yet subjected to control operations will be kept under close surveillance. Biological studies of the effects of spraying operations in New Brunswick and Quebec will be continued.
Has the minister anything about the pine shoot moth?

No, I understand we have nothing on it here.

Supply-Agriculture
Has there been any work done on it? I understand that a considerable amount of work has been done on this in southwestern Ontario.
I think that work is largely being done by the Ontario government, but we can get information on it.
Probably the minister's department is doing a considerable amount of work on it too.
We may be, but the work that is done on all these is really being done by the provincial government.
The minister gave quite a good report on it last year. That is why I say he must have something about it. He can get the information on it later if he wishes.
If we can get the information here, we shall; if not, we can get it from the people who have it.

Can the
minister report any progress in arresting the spread of the Dutch elm disease?

While the minister is checking that, I may say that I notice in the details under forest biology that we have provision for five cooks and one cookee. I was wondering how the one cookee was distributed among the five cooks. Who is the lucky cook who is going to get the cookee, and who are the ones that are going to be without?
Of course, the explanation of that is that probably in most of the camps where they have cooks the cook does all the work, but there is probably one camp that is so big that they need a cookee.
The Minister has not yet answered my question about the Dutch elm disease.

We have just sent for the expert on that. I understand that that is being handled, as I said a moment ago, by the province and by the cities in general where they are dealing with the problem. Of course, we carry on research work and give any information we can with regard to those matters, but I understand it is primarily carried on by the provinces and by the cities. Item agreed too.
It- Plant protection, $839,688.
I should like to ask the minister whether this has to do with weed control.
It does not have to do with weed control. It has to do with the inspection of plants, insects and diseases that effect nursery stock coming in, as to what may be carried by that stock.
It has nothing to do with spraying and so on?

It is not the spraying; it is checking the plants that come in. When you come to the boundary line coming from the United States, if you have plants, sometimes you have difficulty in getting across and they insist on your destroying them before you come in. That is part of the protection against bringing in disease. We also inspect what is going out.

I wonder whether the minister could give us some information regarding the importation of balled burlapped evergreens from Holland and the danger of nematode infestation, of which all nurserymen are so much afraid? I understand there is some reciprocal agreement with the government of Holland that they will not ship out anything that is infected. I wonder what this government has to do with that arrangement. Has there been any difficulty with the government of Holland regarding the importation of these balled burlapped evergreens?

That is true. We send inspectors to Holland at times to make inspections before the plants leave there to come here. We have reciprocal arrangements with a number of countries, Holland being one of them. For example, we get many bulbs from Holland. We have arrangements with countries from which we receive considerable numbers of plants so that we can make inspections there before the plants are sent here.

It is a little different in the case of bulbs. I understand that this nematode is carried only when there is soil along with the plant; it is carried in the soil. I wonder whether there has been any trouble or whether any importations have been stopped because of nematodes found in the soil.

There have been cases where plants have been prevented from coming here on that account, but I have not the information here in regard to that. Of course, if it were not for the danger of infestation, we would not have started that at the time. The fact that we have the inspection results in some plants being prevented from coming.

Along that line, I might mention an experience I had. At the time of the coronation two English

oaks were brought into my home village from England. They were from an area where there was infestation of the nematode, and the requirement was that all soil was to be washed from the roots, and then they were shipped out in a bag by air mail. The interesting part was that all the soil had to be removed.

Item agreed to.
Experimental farms service-
12. Experimental farms service administration, $211,122.

I should like to ask the
minister whether a spray has been discovered that will kill chicory, or blue devil as it is commonly called in my part of the country.
There is one under development at Lacombe, Alberta, that is giving hopeful signs, but it has not yet been proven and therefore it is not being recommended or distributed.

I should like to raise a point under item 12 which ties in with the science service. In many cases the science service and the experimental farms service follow parallel lines. The one aspect of that with which I am familiar is the very contentious one of weed control. We have, in the science service, personnel working on one aspect of weed control and in the experimental farms service individuals at the experimental farms who are carrying out limited projects within their own jurisdiction. I think this same principle is duplicated in many of the projects which are carried out. In addition, we find that both of the services, the science service and the experimental farms service, compete for technical personnel to carry on their projects. I wonder whether the minister has ever given serious consideration to a long run trend of amalgamating these two services and perhaps part of the economics division so that you would have an integrated service whereby you would carry out your technical surveys under the science service, investigate them through the experimental farms service and carry out the research work through the economics division. I think such a trend deserves very serious consideration and I would appreciate having the minister's comment on the suggestion.

I understand that what my hon. friend has in mind is presumed to be already taken care of. There is an eastern committee and a western committee already set up. There are representatives representing the federal services and others representing the provincial services. They review all the representations that are made to them and determine whether a certain thing is to be
Supply-Agriculture
given to the science service or is to be handled by the experimental farms. In other words, they designate where it can be best dealt with and it is there it is dealt with. This distribution to the services is made before the actual problem is dealt with either by the one or the other. I presume at times there will be co-operation between the two in dealing with a problem.

I think we should go one step further and have one technical officer in charge of the three departments with a representative from the science service and from the experimental farms service. I believe we would have closer co-operation once projects are started. I agree, as the minister pointed out, that before a project is launched there is co-operation between the departments but once a project is launched difficulty arises, and I think that by closer mechanical co-ordination of the services we would have a more efficient organization. I wish the minister would give that serious consideration.
We will give it serious consideration. I will ask the officials to have a look at it and take what is in Hansard.

In view of the fact that the central experimental farm cannot expand any farther on account of the building projects surrounding it, has the minister given any consideration to expanding the farm by way of an annex say 50 or 75 miles from the central farm?

This question, of course, as to what is going to become of the experimental farm in Ottawa comes up nearly every year. The department is of the opinion that it ought to remain just where it is. We do not think it is going to help agriculture or help anyone who comes here to get an idea of what is going on in Canada to have the experimental farm 20 miles away from Ottawa or even 10 miles away. We think one of the chief assets of our experimental farm system as well as one of the chief assets of the city of Ottawa and of Canada in general is the central experimental farm right where it is.
This question came up recently when the city wanted to take a piece of it to make a highway, and we insisted on its being just as small a piece as they could get along with and still have the highway. We intend to continue that policy. We are not making any preparations to take anything away from the present experimental farm and we hope the farm will always remain just where it is. It may be possible that at some time in the future we will have to have another location for some particular things that we

Supp ly-A griculture
cannot do right here in the centre of the city but we are not considering that at the moment.

I did not have reference to discarding the farm in Ottawa. I was speaking about an annex. We know that as time goes on and the years go by we must expand in every department. There is no room for expansion of the farm in Ottawa and I had in mind what the department would do if it wanted to expand it. When I asked the question I also had in mind certain fruits, vegetables and so on with respect to which a much better job of experimenting could probably be done in a slightly warmer climate. I have in mind the region along the St. Lawrence river and naturally Leeds county and the fact that a slightly warmer climate would be helpful in the case of experiments with some small fruits and types of flowers. We know the climate is warmer along the St. Lawrence river than at Ottawa, and perhaps a better job of experimenting could be done if an annex were established there.

Can the minister give a report to the committee on the latest information he has respecting the new breed of hog known as the Lacombe? I think you must have raised seven generations now and you should be able to tell us whether the outlook is as hopeful this year as it was last year when you reported on the experiment being made.

We had that same breed of hog at Ottawa when I came here 20 years ago and we had some very lively discussions in the house on it. I think most of the people who were interested in carrying the project still further were on this side of the house at that time, and we had to explain what had happened up to that time. Last year I took the trouble to go and look at the hogs at Lacombe myself and when I was there I asked the direct question: Is there any difference at all between this experiment and the one carried on at Ottawa 20 years ago? The answer was no. I had a look at the hogs and all I wish to say at this time is that it will probably be wise to distribute them some time, but I think there has got to be a lot of preparatory educational work done among the people whom we persuaded to put the long white hog all the way across this country. Breeders are established everywhere across the country. They have that type of hog, and in the face of that I do not think it should be the work of the department to go out and say that there is another one that is better until we have proven it to their satisfaction. I have grave doubts whether it is better. Hog breeders

outside the service altogether to whom I have been talking do not think it is better yet, and until they do I would not be in favour of making any great distribution of the hogs.

That is why I asked the question. I have great faith in the Yorkshire hog myself. However, I have an open mind on the matter, and if you can show me that by doing this experimental work you can produce a better hog than the Yorkshire hog and get a bacon hog that this country wants I would be all for it. I have another question while I am on my feet. Most hog feeders know that fishmeal is a valuable food. I think it is in Nova Scotia that they are producing fishmeal silage now. It is a wonderful thing when you are feeding hogs but the trouble is you have got to inform the hog feeder that he can only feed fishmeal up to a certain point. If you feed it right along you are going to destroy the business of the packing companies because you will have to put in the frying pan bacon that will taste fishy. You have got to be very careful about that. I think it should be a part of the work of the department to carry on an educational program. They should see that in every bag of such meal that goes out there should be information to the effect that if you feed it too long you will destroy the thing that everybody is trying to achieve, an ideal bacon hog producing bacon with a first class flavour.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.
Just when the committee rose for lunch I was going to ask the minister whether they were still experimenting with the scrub hogs they had out at the experimental farm a couple of years ago.
I have not seen the scrub hogs. They are experimenting with some very good ones.

It all depends on what you call "good". Anything that I saw was not good. Perhaps they had some good ones but I did not happen to see them. The ones I saw were anything but good. They were a cross or something with Chester Whites. I do not know what they were trying to do with them.

I think that might be something along the lines of the experiment we were talking about at Lacombe with Chester Whites, Berks and Yorks and by certain methods of crossing trying to develop a new strain.
I understood that this La-combe breed was all in the west. I understood that there was not any of that breed down here at all. Is that not true?
There are a few at the Ottawa farm with lopped ears hanging down over their eyes.
They might just be the first cross. Are there any of the Lacombe breed here in Ottawa at the experimental farm?

The breed which was here 20 years ago is the same breed as is at Lacombe now. At least the experts tell me out there it is. I have been over at the Ottawa farm within the last two weeks and have seen some similar ones there, as my hon. friend from Huron has no doubt seen. I do not know just how they got there but they are there.

If the ones out west are supposed to be the Lacombe breed, and as to which I understand they are trying to get registered now-there is an application before the government to have them registered -I sincerely suggest that if they are as bad as the ones out at the farm here, they had probably better disregard registration.

It has gone further than that. There has been an application for registration and I am not sure that arrangements have not been made to have them registered. They have asked me if they are to be distributed and I have not agreed. That is what I have been telling the committee.

We shall let that matter
drop for the moment. I want to add a word to what the hon. member for Leeds said about the experimental farm. I brought this matter up a couple of years ago, I think, when there was some discussion at that time, as there has been every year about moving the farm out of the city of Ottawa. I understand that there is now some discussion with regard to moving the barns and the housing for the animals out further from the city. That would split up the animal research division or the livestock division and the crops division. That is to say, the crop experimental work would be maintained here on the present farm but the animal experimentation work would be moved out of the city. I can see a certain amount of justification for such a move if the city by-law prohibited the keeping of animals within the city limits. In that case you might be obliged to move them out. I wonder whether there is any truth in the suggestion that such a move is to take place?

As I said before lunch, we have not agreed to any proposal to move any of the experimental farm out of Ottawa. So
Supply-Agriculture
far as the department is concerned and so far as the government is concerned, the farm is to remain just as it is and where it is. I cannot say what will be the situation 25 years from now. My hon. friend might be in office by that time, I do not know.

I do not wish to be misunderstood. I am not suggesting that it be moved out of Ottawa. I am just wondering whether there has been any discussion taking place between the department and the city or whoever the discussion was with, with regard to the matter. I can see the one thing that might conflict and that is if the city by-law says-and I imagine that it does-provided that no animals be kept within its boundaries, referring to cows, horses or pigs. I suppose such animals as cats and dogs would not be affected. But in view of that possibility, there might have been some discussions at least. Have there been any discussions with the city of Ottawa?

There is a discussion about moving part or all of the experimental farm out every time they want to build a new public building in Ottawa. Somebody comes down here and says, "We would like to build it on the experimental farm". When they wanted a place to practise tennis they wanted it out there. We get those suggestions all the time. Discussion comes up every time somebody has a notion of that kind. The government has always taken the position that there is going to be no moving of the experimental farm.

I should like to ask the minister whether the Lacombe hogs are being bred only in the one place. When I drive home from Ottawa is there some place to which I can go and see them or must I go to Lacombe to see them?

The only place I am sure I have seen them is at Lacombe. You can see hogs in different stages of the cross breeding which is taking place to produce what is known as the Lacombe hog. All I know is this; there are a few lop-eared hogs at the Ottawa farm. I did not go in and ask about them. I go out to the experimental farm here occasionally, and in driving through there within the last two or three weeks I have seen a few hogs that look very much like those I saw at Lacombe. I therefore would not deny that some of them are there. However, I would not say they are there officially.

How many generations have
been developed now by the gentlemen who run the minister's department?

I am not certain as to how many generations they have gone through but I think you will find out that they are

Supply-Agriculture
at different stages with those hogs. There are hogs there that conform more to the Berks in appearance but they are white and there are hogs that conform more to the Chester White. In other words, I would think their work with the breeding system that is being followed has not been completed in order to produce a hog that I would want to accept as of established type.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
On this item I should like to
interject a remark or two. I myself made a special trip to the Lacombe farm last summer. While I did not have anyone show me around, I saw a number of pigs which I presume are this new strain of Lacombe hogs that are being produced by the experimental farm system. I have no remarks to make about that matter except to say that they looked like a rugged type of hog. Perhaps the one advantage of their having ears hanging down over their eyes was that they could not so conveniently squeeze through garden fences. I think the point that we would be mostly interested in with regard to this particular experiment is whether or not the experiment has been successful in fixing the type of a good, rugged, economically produced hog. I think that is the essential thing that we are all striving for. It will take time to determine whether or not that is an animal superior to the standard breeds of hogs that we have had in this country for a long time.
I should like just to go on and say another word or two in connection with this vote which I note is up $27,000 from last year. In any little opportunity I have to wander around the country, I am always glad of the chance of dropping in on an experimental farm. It has always been a pleasant experience and there is something there which one can pick up every time he goes there. I think our experimental farms throughout the country are a credit to those who have been responsible for their organization and administration. More than that, I think that agriculture as an industry deserves that type of governmental scientific assistance. I commend most warmly the foresight of those who developed this system and who have been in each instance attempting to carry on experimental work which they thought would be of value to the particular community in which those farms were located. Perhaps I might be forgiven if I digressed for a moment, but I think what I am going to refer to is sufficiently close to this problem to ensure that I will not be ruled out of order for so doing. A few weeks ago I had the pleasure and privilege of attending the fiftieth anniversary of the first agricultural

college established in the three western provinces, namely the institution in the province of Manitoba.
May I digress to say that it was a very creditable jubilee celebration which brought together 1,200 or 1,500 students who had attended the old agricultural college over the past 50 years. May I say, Mr. Chairman, that the man who was given the privilege of lifting the first sod towards the construction of a new science building, to which the graduates of that institution are making quite a reasonable contribution, was also the man first to register at that institution in 1906. Later, I had the privilege of listening to the dean of our agricultural college, who happens to be a namesake of mine, make a splendid address. In passing I should like to refer to that, having in mind particularly what agriculture is facing up to in this very competitive industrial world today. I am one of those who firmly believe that, more and more, agriculture has to look to our scientifically trained men to give the leadership, not only in production, but also in marketing and all these other fields that pertain to an industry of the importance of agriculture in this country.
Whatever government can do through experimental farms, through their various science divisions and their universities, to train agriculturists in a manner to enable them to give that leadership, I think it will be money well spent in the interests of this country in the days to come. For that reason I am glad to see that this vote is being continued and somewhat increased. In our own province of Manitoba we have two institutions that are very well regarded. I am referring to the experimental farm at Brandon and the one at Morden. They are carrying on in somewhat different fields, but none the less they are looked to by the people in those communities as well as the people outside of those communities for guidance and for information on any particular problem that may be affecting any farmer who is interested in improving his position.
We have in addition to that, as everyone knows, in all communities men who are giving a great deal of attention to the advancement of agriculture in the matter of producing of select stock seed, improving varieties and expanding these things as well as developing new crops and testing them out. Every community has such people who are a very valuable addition to our background in trying to establish agriculture scientifically on a sounder basis. I am thinking for the moment, if I may, of another area, partly in my own constituency, where the conditions are quite different from those that

might be associated with the farms at Brandon or at Morden. In this area there is a different type of soil and, to some extent, different climatic conditions. These people seem to feel that they should have some direction in the way of developing speciality crops, whether that be corn, grasses and clover or things of that nature, I do not know. Nevertheless, the feeling is there and they think-I am speaking now of the local board of trade, the farmers union organization and other groups of that kind-that something by way of an illustration or demonstration plot should be established where people could go by and see what could be done. It might be a useful instrument in giving a lead perhaps to a more stable type of agriculture in that community. I think the minister will recognize the area to which I am referring and he will recall having met with a group of people from the McCreary area a year or so ago. I am just putting that before him and I would be interested in knowing what progress might have been made, if any, towards reviewing the possibility of some development of that nature.
I would only add one other word. When I referred to agricultural graduates, and I was not confining that to Manitoba alone, when I met with my associates of former years at this celebration, I want to say to the minister that quite a number of them were associated with the experimental farm system in various parts of this country.
May I tell my hon. friend that surveys are now being made in connection with the McCreary proposal.

I have only a few remarks to make on this item. I am very glad to see this increase which, as the hon. member who has just spoken said, is about $27,400. I only hope that the $27,400 is to be used to establish an experimental farm in the Medicine Hat area. As the minister knows, we now have irrigation right down to Medicine Hat. At the present time we have an experimental range station at Manyberries, which is 75 miles south of Medicine Hat. We have an experimental station at Lethbridge-
It is a farm.

Perhaps you are right, but it is 100 miles from Medicine Hat. However, we do feel that, now that we have irrigation right at our doorstep, serious consideration should be given to the establishment of an experimental farm in the Medicine Hat area.
I am sure the minister has had some representations, not only from me but from others, with regard to the establishment of that station. I do hope that in the very near future consideration will be given to an
Supply-Agriculture
experimental farm in the Medicine Hat area. I might also say this. We are in a very dry area which now has irrigation. These farmers really do not know how to handle the water that we have today. The peculiar thing is that then the water was turned into the ditches about the middle of last month, it started to rain and it has been raining ever since. We hope it keeps up. However, I think that what we should have in the Medicine Hat area is an experimental farm to which the farmers can go to see how the different crops are raised. There are many crops that can be raised in that area, as the minister knows. I think it is time consideration was given to that idea.
I want to ask the minister one question. Have any representations been made to him by the city, by the chamber of commerce or by anyone but me, from the Medicine Hat area, about the establishment of an experimental farm in that area.

I do not recall, Mr. Chairman, that there is any correspondence on the matter but I was in Medicine Hat not very long ago, as my hon. friend knows, and representations were made at that time by all those organizations. I explained to them, of course, that the Manyberries farm south of Medicine Hat is still operating, which has to do with the dry area rather than the irrigated area, and that we are also carrying on at Vauxhall what we look upon as more or less of a model in connection with irrigation. We have there a very considerable illustration station which is operated for exactly the purpose the hon. member has in mind. The whole project, however, is one that was laid out entirely by our engineers and those who have had great experience in irrigation work and the public does visit that place quite regularly because of the nature of it. I think it does perform much of the irrigation work which might be carried out if we had an experimental farm as such set up. I have some doubt as to whether there is necessity for going farther than that at the present time. Nevertheless, I am pleased to have the representations that were made, and we shall look into the whole matter.

Mr. Chairman, may I take up a few more minutes of the time of the committee? I am sure everyone in the Medicine Hat area appreciates what the dominion government has done with the range experimental farm at Manyberries. Hobart Peters, who is in charge at the present time, has done a very good job, but it is more in the nature of the production of livestock. They have various cattle

Supply-Agriculture
down there that they experiment with. They investigate the number of cattle that each quarter section or section will carry in that area. They have done a wonderful job and they are still doing a wonderful job. They had a range station day out there last week or the week before, and 1,200 people attended. It is a wonderful thing to go down into an area where there are no trees except around a few farm homes, and there are very few there now. At the dominion range station they have shown what can be done by the storage of water. I was going to speak on this on the P.F.R.A. item- perhaps I should when it is mentioned. I think we see the results of a good range experimental farm. We do not go out to Vauxhall because it is 60, 70 or 80 miles away from Medicine Hat. The people just do not go out there, that is all. What we would like to have in Medicine Hat is something the same as they have in Lethbridge, namely, a dominion experimental farm to which the citizens of Medicine Hat could go after a drive of about 10 minutes. That is our idea. We would like that not only for the people living in Medicine Hat but also for the farmers in that area.

I have a question I would like to ask the minister on this item.
I am wondering whether he would like to bring us up to date on the disease-resisting project in Fredericton having to do with experiments into the disease of potatoes?
I think they call it a potato breeding project. How are they coming along with their experiments in Keswick, Kathadin, Canso and Netted Gems? Could we have that information?

While the officials are looking into this question I might answer a question which was asked by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings before lunch. He asked about the cost of operating the Department of Agriculture units at Kent-ville, Nova Scotia. For 1955-56, experimental farm, $188,000; botany and plant pathology, $46,820; entomology, $90,480.
Then, there was a further question asked with regard to the pine shoot moth. An active research program is being maintained on this pest in Ontario. Chemical control is being tested and parasites are being imported this year from Europe in an effort to check the outbreak. Work is going forward at Belleville, Maple and Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario.
A question was asked with regard to grain mites. These were thoroughly investigated during the second world war and it was found that infestations arose mainly from storing grain when the moisture content was
	'	!
excessive or from leaking granaries that permitted damp spots to develop. Chemical control is effective.
In recent years emphasis has been on the rusty grain beetle which has been the principal pest in stored grain. Research is continuing to improve the effect of insecticides when used in large bins. This work is centred at Winnipeg.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the statements made by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa regarding the splendid work done at the dominion experimental farm at Morden, Manitoba. This farm is in my constituency, and I know from first-hand knowledge the high calibre of people employed there and the splendid contribution they have made to agriculture and also to horticulture. They are to be commended for the splendid work they have done in horticultural research in that part of western Canada.
While I am on this point I wonder whether the minister can tell me the name of the man who has been appointed as the new superintendent for that farm?

Well, a selection has been indicated but it is before the appeal board at present, and a final decision has not been made as to who is to follow Mr. Leslie.
On the national potato breeding project at Fredericton, two varieties were released. Canso and Keswick were resistant to late blight, but new races of blight have attacked them. Breeding is continuing to try to deal with the new condition which has arisen. It is much the same in principle at the rust. There is a new one.
May I have some information on the Netted Gems?

Yes. They have been grown mainly in the west up to now. They are a very high starch content potato and are being introduced into New Brunswick largely with the idea of providing a potato that is suitable for potato chips.

While we are on this item may I say that the station at Summerland, British Columbia, is a very fine one of which we are very proud. At the station there is a dairy herd. I should like to call the minister's attention to the fact that Summerland is only about 7| miles north of Penticton, which is the centre of the fruit-growing industry. The dairying activities are centred about 40 miles north between Kelowna and Vernon or even north of that again. I suggest therefore that this herd is not well placed. I understand that representations have been made to the department to have the herd moved

from the station at Summerland to a more northerly position in the Vernon district. Has any examination of that situation occurred?
That is under consideration at the present time but it has not yet been determined what will take place.

I should like to commend the department and the minister for having set up an experimental station in the Vegreville constituency to deal with a particular soil problem. There are millions of acres of what is known as burnt-out or solonetz soil. This has always been a problem and nobody seems to have found the answer as to the best way to deal with this type of soil. A farmer may spend a lot of time, work and money trying to build up this soil and find his returns are not very good.
That was the purpose of setting up this experimental station and it has met with a lot of enthusiasm throughout Alberta and I think throughout Canada among soil specialists. I realize that they have a great job ahead of them in their efforts to find an answer to the best way to deal with this type of soil. I am sure that once an answer is found it will prove to be of great value to the people of Alberta as well as to the people of Canada.
Some work has been done this year and they are going to hold a field day on August 7. I have invited the minister to attend and I should like to see the deputy minister and other officials of the department as well as the parliamentary assistant there on that day. It would do the parliamentary assistant a lot of good to visit western Canada.
So far there has been no superintendent appointed at this farm. I understand that efforts are being made to find a top soil expert to work there. Also the program should be expanded. I shall not go into the details but I simply wanted to make these few comments.

Could the minister give some information as to the progress being made in establishing an illustration station in the Crystal City-Clearwater area in Manitoba. I had some communication with the minister in regard to this matter and I am wondering how it is progressing.
No further progress has been made since we were discussing it before. We have not yet selected any place there for a demonstration station.

Apparently everyone wants an experimental station in his area. A peculiar type of soil is found in the area around The Pas and across the border in the Carrot river area of Saskatchewan and I understand that
Supply-Agriculture
at one time the government was considering establishing an experimental farm in The Pas area. Is the establishment of such a farm under consideration at the present time?

There are considerable developments taking place in the Carrot river area both on the Manitoba and Saskatchewan sides of the boundary. Beyond the work which is being carried on there, no undertaking has been given up to the present time to put in a special illustration station. There is always a possibility that with the conditions which will develop when the drainage and diking system which is being put in goes ahead there may be a necessity for it.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister could give us any information in connection with any experimentation that has been undertaken with respect to the feeding of wheat to hogs? I understand that there is a method being used by which the wheat content of the feeding formula can be increased greatly. I think every farmer knows that ordinarily you cannot feed much more than one-third wheat.

The general experience is that you cannot use more than one-third wheat in the grain mix when the hog has reached a certain stage in development. As my hon. friend knows, wheat has been fed to hogs in western Canada for a long time and it has been an important part of the mix. But care must be taken in feeding it, particularly if the hogs are confined to pens and not able to get out and run around a little. They are more likely to stiffen up if they are fed more wheat when they cannot run around outside.
Experiments are being carried on at all experimental farms and stations, and I am sure that nearly every farmer, particularly those in the west, is carrying on experiments as well.

I do
not know whether my information is authentic, but I have been told that some western hog feeders are feeding practically 100 per cent wheat successfully in the finishing of hogs. I was just wondering if that was the result of experiments by one of the branches of the department or by a private firm which has perhaps developed a supplement in order that a greater amount of wheat may be fed.

I cannot say that advice has been given that wheat alone could be fed under all circumstances and conditions. Frozen and rusted wheat and wheat of poor quality is being fed quite generally. I remember once driving into the yard of a man in the middle of Saskatchewan who had some of the

Supply-Agriculture
finest pigs I have seen running around the yard. I asked him how he got his pigs in that shape and he said, "Come, I will show you." He had them eating whole wheat out of a trough filled to the top with water, the wheat being in the bottom. I went back to the agricultural department in Regina, that being the closest point, knowing they had a lot of good information, and I told them what I had seen. They asked me whether the hogs were running around the yard, and I told them they were. They told me that if those pigs had been closed up in a pen and fed like that they would probably have stiffened up and been unable to move. I find in our own experience in feeding hogs that you can feed more wheat to them if they are running outside than you can to hogs that are penned up. No doubt farmers in general find that out.
In view of the remarks the minister made regarding the Lacombe breed of hogs, I wonder whether he would tell us who has made the application to have these hogs registered.

The people breeding them on farms. They want to get them up to standard and they think they have a considerable number of them up to a standard where the breed is stabilized so that if you carry on on that basis you will get the hogs bred back to similar types. Some of them advocating that have in mind crossing them with some other breed of hog such as a York. Some of them do not say that the breed is so well established that you can be absolutely certain that they will breed back in type, but they say that if you cross them in a certain way with another breed of hog you will get a more rugged type and a hog that will produce more what you desire. They are trying to get a big ham with small shoulders and keep a considerable length to the hog at the same time. In other words, they are trying to get a hog more like the Danish and Swedish hogs without having them exactly the same, one that is more suitable to this country.

I take it that some of the breeders who are working on this are not agreed as to whether or not they should be registered. As I understand it, the minister is not sure he is agreed either. From what he has said, it is not likely at this time that he is going to accept them for registration.

The national livestock records people have the suggestion before them now, but even if they were recognized as a breed the department would have to come to a conclusion as to whether we would promote their distribution right across the country

in competition with the white Yorks, we have already spread right across the country.
I take it that the minister thinks further experimentation should be done before this is done.
Yes.

The minister and I have had some differences of opinion on a number of occasions regarding the position of the farms. If my hon. friend had been listening last night, he would have found out that there are quite a number of them right across the country now. Last night questions were asked as to how returned men had got along paying for their farms. If I remember correctly, there were only 69 out of 2,637 who had not been able to take care of all their indebtedness in connection with their farms up to the present time since the war.

But I should just like to point out that there are some people who make a success of farming under the conditions we have had and I do not think there are very many who would not agree that if they could not make a success of farming under these conditions they probably would not under any.

It is true that the property at one time belonged to the province and there was an arrangement made whereby the federal government took over the experimental farm. There was one building which was built on land that belonged to the province. The title to that land has also been turned over to the federal government, so we have all the titles now as far as we know.

Mr.	Chairman, I	want to
speak for a few moments on a question that		

I am quite sure will appeal to the minister as a member of a Christian church and a practising Christian, except temporarily possibly at election time, and perhaps we are all sinners in that respect. Anyway, I hope the item I wish to mention will appeal to his Christian conscience and give him a further opportunity to practice those principles in which he believes.
The subject I wish to mention is the question of the humane slaughter of animals, a question which is receiving wider interest across the country every year. The reason most Canadians have not been interested in the matter is that they do not know the facts. They do not know about the cruelty that exists in our packing houses across the country and almost to the same extent in the United States.
The reason they are beginning to know is the good work done by various organizations and associations which have given some consideration to the question, studied methods of killing, written pamphlets and taken their time to acquaint their fellow citizens with the situation that exists in so-called Christian Canada. The matter has received a particular amount of attention in British Columbia, and on that account a committee of the society for the prevention of cruelty to animals went before the agriculture committee of the provincial legislature and made a very good case indeed. Their representations had a great effect on all members of the committee, regardless of party. They were so impressed and affected that when the representations had been completed the committee adopted the following paragraph in its report to the legislature, as found in a news letter of the humane slaughter association:
On February 29, 1956, following representations by the S.P.C.A. and our own association-
That is the humane slaughter association.
-the select standing committee on agriculture of the provincial legislature reported as follows:
"Your committee heard representations from the humane slaughter society, the society for the prevention of cruelty to animals and the Canadian association of packers with regard to the merits of humane slaughtering of food animals and the difficulties arising from such methods. After due consideration, your committee recommends as follows:
The committee expresses sympathy with the ideas expressed by the humane slaughter society and strongly recommends that the federal and provincial departments of agriculture make a thorough study of all aspects dealing with this question with the object of putting into effect the most humane methods possible in the killing of food animals."
This is a question that has received a great deal of attention in the United States and by a number of very prominent congressmen who are concerned about our present inhumane methods. Just to indicate the interest

I am going to quote from two or three news articles in this connection. The first is an editorial in the Detroit Free Press of June 5, 1956, in which I find the following:
A measure of civilization's height is the degree to which it puts aside barbarism and cruelty in all their aspects. If means for slaughtering livestock are available which will stop any present suffering by the slaughtered animals, it seems to us that the civilized thing to do is require their employment.
Then we have the New York Daily Mirror of June 22, 1956. In an editorial it had this to say:
Packers from Finland to Fiji have installed humane killing devices that make our slaughter houses look and sound like medieval dungeons.
.	.	. Something deeper than a squeamish repugnance toward blood motivates those who would see swift reform. It is the abiding conviction that callous brutality has no place in our society.
Then I refer to another editorial in the Christian Science Monitor of March 16, 1956, containing these words:
Bills are pending before the committees of both the Senate and the House of Representatives to require humane slaughtering in the United States.
In the issue of May 31, 1956, I find the following:
Most Americans would be surprised to learn that the United States is a backward country, in one respect at least. It is 25 to 50 years behind many European countries in the development of humane methods of commercial animal slaughter.
The same applies to Canada at this time.
I am not going to detain the committee longer. I have simply mentioned the matter and brought the facts to the minister's attention. I should like him to tell the committee what representations he has received and what his department intends to do to bring us at least up to the standard of the Fiji islanders in this respect.

There have been representations made to the department. The officials have been gathering information from countries like Sweden, Denmark, Britain, the United States and elsewhere as to what is being done in those countries, and they are accumulating as much information as possible before making any decision with regard to the matter.
The matter is under serious consideration?
Yes, and has been for the last six months.

Is the minister going to comment on the matter I brought to his attention on the first item, regarding the administration of the production service and having the veterinary services under the production service? I see that well over $6 million, and it is well over, out of a total 67509-378

of $11,207,835 has to do with veterinary services, either research or disease work. I wonder whether the minister would give us some idea of his feelings in this regard, and tell us what is the policy of the government at this time.

The amalgamation of these two branches is to be made on the first of April next. It is now being worked out and will be brought to completion around that time. I refer to the health of animals and pathological divisions.
As a separate branch?
They will still be under production services.

I take it that animal disease research work and disease work are to come under one head but still under production service. I sincerely suggest that is not what the veterinary association has requested. I can see very little advantage in doing that. As I say, I do not want anybody to misinterpret my words as being directed personally to anybody in the department. However, it is the feeling of veterinarians across this country that they probably could be of better service to the nation if there were one separate branch of animal disease services or veterinary services or whatever you want to call it. They think it would be better if the two branches or divisions were in one separate branch, whereby the head of that branch would go directly to the deputy minister rather than having to go through a layman to get to the deputy minister.
That is the feeling among the veterinarians across the nation. I sincerely suggest that the minister give further consideration to the proposal, and that rather than just bring them in under the production services he make a separate branch of the department having to do with animal diseases or animal research and diseases.

When I came to the department over 20 years ago that is as it was except that both these divisions were separate 20 years ago, as I recall it; it may have been less than that or it may have been a little more. These different branches reported directly to the minister or to the deputy minister. I reorganized the department to put it as it is now, in five divisions the head of each reports directly to the deputy or to myself. The two branches that are referred to are under production services; that is, they will be under production services under the new set-up.
We think it is the better way to have it and we do not think we should start to get back to where we were previously. There

Supply-Agriculture
are many other divisions in this department which think they too should have the privilege of dealing direct. Whenever anything important comes up and they require to bring it to either the deputy or the minister, of course they are free to bring it. But when we get together groups to discuss what we are going to do by way of policy and so on, we deal directly with about half a dozen people instead of dealing with every branch in the department. It does not work in with the general organization of the department to have that particular section reporting directly through the veterinary director general. It does not suit the set-up of the department in general to have that made special.
I may say that I get requests from people outside of the department every once in a while that a certain person with whom they come in contact from time to time be put into the position of dealing directly with the minister or the deputy minister. On those occasions I have taken the position that the way in which the department is organized- and we think it is a better system of organization than was there previously-

The position here is not quite the same as it is elsewhere. I would suggest that this is a little different, because you are dealing with one aspect of the livestock industry in this nation, namely the health of animals. I do not think the minister could mention another part of his department that is comparable, where you have two separate divisions. Now he says they are to be brought into one but still under another head, and it will be between the director of the two divisions and the deputy minister.
This is one of the most important branches of the whole department, I would suggest, because when the health of animals is to be considered it is a matter of great importance, as we all know after what we went throguh in 1952. The production service is an extremely important branch. As I said, I realize that quite a bit over half of that work now has directly to do with the health of the animal population of this country. Hence it is quite an arguing point to have a separate branch when there are other branches that spend very little more-no, not any more; there is one other branch that spends less, as a matter of fact, than the animal pathology branch and health of animals, compensation for animals-than does this branch. So I hope the minister will give further consideration to this suggestion. I am sure he will hear further from the Canadian veterinary association with regard to this matter.

There has been considerable controversy particularly over two diseases. One is rabies, with regard to which I want to commend the department for looking after us very well. The other is scrapie disease in sheep. A great many stories are going around. How much truth there is in them I should not like to say. In view of the fact that very little is known about the disease of scrapie in sheep, I think probably it is one of the most important things the health of animals branch has to deal with at the present time; also in view of the fact that there are still in the country many suspected sheep that have come from flocks that have since been destroyed. A great many of these sheep are scattered around various districts in Canada. They are not even all under surveillance. We assume, however, that most of them would be under surveillance.
In view of the fact that so little is known about the disease I would sincerely suggest that the department should be taking into serious consideration the setting up of some research, or else taking the results of the research of other countries such as England, for instance, where you would think they would know more about this disease inasmuch as they have had to deal with it much longer than have we, and co-operating closely with the department in England along that line.
The disease could be very costly to the sheep industry. I am not sure about this, but I understand that one entire flock was destroyed last year. If they pay as much for all sheep as was paid for that particular flock, I say that it could be very costly, because I understand the amount was up almost in the $100,000 bracket for some 600 head of sheep. I do not know where I would ever be able to find a flock of sheep, counting the lambs and all, that would average anywhere near that price. I wonder whether the minister could give us some assurance that all the stories we hear are not true,

and whether he could tell us what the department is doing in this regard. As I say, it is a very serious matter and is looked upon as being a very serious matter by the sheep breeders across the country. As a matter of fact they do not know where they are going. They do not know how many sheep they can export or when they can export and when they cannot.
