Before the minister replies to this question dealing with scrapie, may I point out that we in Alberta are very much concerned about the appearance of this disease amongst the sheep flocks of the province. I have in my hand an item taken from the Manitoba Co-operator which deals with the scrapie outbreak to some extent, and I should like to read a brief section of this article which is referring to Dr. Swales, who I believe was at one time associated with the Department of Agriculture as an animal pathologist:
The incident Dr. Swales referred to was a purebred flock in the Ottawa valley of Ontario. About 1947 Scrapie was found in it and was traced to an imported ram. The flock was destroyed and compensation paid.
If that report is true, then this outbreak of scrapie that occurred in Alberta this year is not the first instance of scrapie in Canada. I mentioned that we in Alberta are concerned about this disease. We are particularly concerned about a number of rumours associated with the disposition of the flock of sheep which belonged to Mr. P. J. Rock. Before this question is closed I should like the minister to inform us as to the number of sheep which were slaughtered and for which the federal government paid compensation, and the amount of compensation paid.
I should like also to have the minister give the committee some assurance that the registrations of the purebred animals, which at this time were slaughtered, have been called in, because there is just the possibility that with a large herd like this being slaughtered some substitutions could be made. I certainly do not believe the minister would want this to happen. I want him to give us assurance that every care was taken to see that the animals paid for were the ones on the registration forms turned in.

As I think is generally
known, Mr. Chairman, scrapie is a disease among sheep which has been known in Great Britain over a very long period, probably 200 years. We have not had a great deal of experience with it here, although we have available to us all the information which is available in Great Britain and elsewhere if they have had it.
In so far as the situation here is concerned, I think it is correct to say that there have been three outbreaks. There were three farmers concerned in the first one and there have been two others. In 1945-46 the number of animals slaughtered was 102. The farmer was Mr. Baldwin, and the amount paid was $2,131.33. Then in the outbreak in 1951-52, which was traceable to the same outbreak, there were 65 sheep belonging to Mr. Tisdale and $2,244 was paid. In 1952-53

Supply-Agriculture
there were some 11 sheep destroyed belonging to Mr. Charter and $525 was paid. Then in 1954-55 Mr. McQuay had 108 slaughtered and the compensation paid was $8,100. Mr. Rock in 1955-56 had 674 sheep slaughtered and they were all registered. There is not any question about them being slaughtered or of their being substitutions. The compensation paid was $100,050. The sheep that had been sold from the flock were all traced and it was proven that there was no scrapie carried along with them into any of the other flocks. I think, therefore, the matter has been pretty well cleared up for the present.
On the questions which were raised by the hon. member for Moose Mountain I think the answers are as follows. Sheep specimens collected in Alberta for the study of scrapie are part of the project to study causative agents of the disease, pathological changes, and the search for sero-aglutination blood tests which would indicate the presence of the disease prior to the establishment of clinical symptoms. The progress of this type of project is invariably slow, for the first thing that must be done is a thorough micropathological examination of the brain and spinal cords. This work is now being done. A search is also under way for a causative agent in the spleen, liver and kidneys, but no results are yet available from this work. Blood samples collected have been separated and the blood serum has been frozen for future use in the establishment of diagnostic tests.

I should like to ask the minister if he can explain the vast difference in prices paid by way of compensation for the sheep that have been slaughtered. For example, I find a rough calculation shows that for the 11 sheep slaughtered in 1952-53 the compensation was approximately $50 a head, while the compensation paid to Mr. Rock was over $100 per head. Why the tremendous spread? Sheep have not changed that much in price, and I take it they were all purebred.

Well, the Rock flock is looked upon, or was looked upon, as one of the best flocks, if not the best flock, in the world in that breed. They were very highly pedigreed. The sheep were being sold not for the ordinary purposes of putting mutton on the market, or lambs on the market, but for breeding purposes at prices higher than the government agreed to pay. As a matter of fact there was considerable negotiating and inspection work done to determine whether this was a reasonable amount, and it was decided that it was.

On my
own responsibility I want to say that I feel there should be a ceiling on the amount of compensation paid to an individual. We should have reasonable compensation. It should meet as nearly as possible the justice of the situation. If a man has high quality stock that must be destroyed, then he should receive reasonable compensation. I wish to join with the hon. member who has just spoken and say that there does seem to be great discrimination in the amounts of payments made for various sheep that have to be slaughtered.
I also want to make a point which I think is borne out by the amount of compensation paid for purebred cattle in the various areas of Saskatchewan at the time of the outbreak of foot and mouth disease. I have heard it said that Mr. Rock is a well-known Liberal in the Drumheller area. Whether or not that has any implications I cannot say, but on my responsibility as a member I say I believe the compensation of $100,000 for 600 sheep perhaps is too large an amount. I think we need to have at least a limit on the amount of compensation paid to one individual. If we have such big operators they should stand a larger amount of the loss. I believe that our smaller operators or smaller farmers are the people who should be looked after and given a chance. If Mr. Rock had that sort of holding he should be in a position to take care of some of his losses.

Mr. Chairman, on the question which is apparently uppermost in my hon. friend's mind, I had not understood that Mr. Rock had always been a Liberal. If he has been a Liberal in recent years it must have been because he, like some other people, was converted to Liberalism. He does not live in Saskatchewan, so it has not concerned me particularly.
Mr. Rock has been one of the outstanding breeders in the province of Alberta, not only of sheep but of cattle. His flock of sheep has been very well known not only in this country and in the United States but also on the continent of Europe. There has been a lot of trading back and forth.
I am not going to argue the question as to whether the sheep were worth that much; I do not know of my own knowledge, but I would like to correct a figure I gave when I spoke on the matter. There were 674 of these sheep. If a person wishes to figure out the actual amount it comes to about $150 for each of them. That price for sheep that were going to be used for mutton, of course, would be a high price. There was not that type of sheep in this flock. It was a very well-bred and highly registered flock of sheep.

It is true there were some lambs. The lambs when they grew would be in the same class as the others. The very best of attention was given to the valuation, and I know that it was gone over very carefully. There was considerable time before an agreement was reached. The final agreement was reached and a settlement was made in accordance with those figures.
How many lambs were in the flock?

I do not know offhand; I have not the information with me. As a matter of fact, I was out there myself in connection with some of the investigations, and men from here were out there. I know that everything possible was done to make that settlement for the slaughter for this very fine flock of sheep as acceptable to everyone concerned as it could possibly be made.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister should be able to give us an approximate idea of the age of the sheep. How many were six months old or under; how many were one year old? That does make a tremendous difference. If you have a flock of 600 sheep and half of them are a year old and another half six months old and you are paying around $160 straight through, I would think that would be an outrageous price.
If my hon. friend will make that notice of question, the information can be made available. It is not here. I will have it brought down in the house on Monday, or just as soon as I can bring it down.
I do not think we need to make it an order for return or anything like that. The minister should bring the information down. That is all that is necessary.

I should like to speak on this matter. I have lived in the same district as Mr. Rock for many years. He is recognized as one of the outstanding breeders, as the minister has pointed out. P. J. Rock and the Grenville brothers are probably the outstanding sheep breeders of western Canada. While $100,000 does seem a very high price to pay in compensation, on the other hand one has to keep in mind the fact that many of Mr. Rock's sheep have been sold at sales for well over $1,000 a head. I remember that one ram sold for $3,000. I do not doubt for one minute that if the flock had been valued in terms of the prices he had received at the purebred stock sales the figure would probably have been considerably in excess of $100,000.
Supply-Agriculture
I understood that the number of sheep was in the neighbourhood of 500. I suppose that during the time the investigation was being made lambing time came around, and no doubt by the end of the consideration that was given to it the number had increased from 500 to 674, on account of the lambs. I believe that the figure that was worked out was worked out on the original basis of the 500 rather than on the 674.
I understand they were all valued individually.

I thought they were figured out on a flock basis rather than on an individual basis. I just wanted to point out that I have been in close contact with both the Rocks and the Grenvilles. I do recognize that they are outstanding breeders, not only of sheep but of shorthorn cattle. They are also outstanding in the grain business.
The Rock farm is not merely a sheep farm; it is a private experimental farm. It has been a show place in western Canada. People come from hundreds of miles away to visit the farm and see the type of work that is being done there with stock. Therefore possibly the price of $100,000 is not out of the way.
As was mentioned, the question of compensation is a difficult one. If in one case a man is paid a very high price and in another case another man is paid a lower price, many people will feel that perhaps there is discrimination. I do not know how much loss an individual farmer is supposed to stand and how much the government is supposed to stand.
Perhaps the minister can explain that point. Is the compensation supposed to represent the actual value of the flock, or is the individual supposed to stand a certain amount of the loss and the government a certain amount? I agree with the minister that actually that flock was probably worth more than $100,000 in terms of the price that could have been received had they been sold at purebred stock shows. I am just wondering whether or not the government does feel that it should pay the full realizable value of the flock?

The valuation of the flock was made by independent valuators who were brought here from the United States to do the job. They valued the sheep at $160,000, and the amount paid was $100,000, which is $60,000 less than the sheep were valued at.

I would like to have some assurance from the minister before we end this discussion that the

Supply-Agriculture
registrations of these purebred animals have been turned in to the department. Have they been turned over?
Yes, they were all turned in to the department.

I have just one comment to make before I sit down. I think the Minister of Agriculture is slipping if he did not visit Moran and find out that Mr. P. J. Rock is one of his supporters. I really believe he had better retire.

The minister gave the
amounts which have been paid, and they indicate that in the case of the first flock of sheep, or the first herd, as the minister refers to them, an average price of $20 was paid; in the case of the next herd the average price was $30; the next one was $40; then in 1952 the average was $80, and now we have $150.
I suggest that this is the only case where anywhere near the actual value has been paid for livestock. Thousands and thousands of animals are killed every year under the instructions of the department because they suffer from infectious diseases, and never before has anywhere near the actual value of the animals been paid. There is supposed to be a limit in the case of sheep under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and there is also a limit for hogs, for cattle, both purebred and grade animals.
Here we have a herd of some 600 sheep.
A flock.

The minister has referred to it as a herd, so we will go along with him on that. The minister does not know how many lambs there were, how many yearlings there were and how many adults there were, but an average price of $150 was paid. I have never seen a flock or herd of animals yet where there was not one animal in the herd which would warrant an extremely high price, say $30,000 or $40,000 in the case of a bull, but the average price for the herd would not be anywhere near that figure. The price for sheep under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act is low in comparison with the price for cattle, but I would say that never in the history of this country have we paid that much for a whole herd of cattle which have been slaughtered under the instructions of the department. I do not think $160 per head has ever been paid for cattle. I should like to know if the meat was used when these sheep were slaughtered, and who got the value of the meat.
They were all buried.

That gets rid of that one then. In the case of cattle it is true that the man gets the value of the meat in the case of
[Mr. Smith (Battle River-Camrose) .1
those not sent to the tank, but I do not think there has ever been a case where a herd of cattle, no matter how good they were, no matter whether they were registered animals, show animals, highly-bred animals, have brought that price as an average for the herd.

In the case of the foot-and-mouth disease the animals were paid for on the basis of the market value, and the price paid was more in the case of purebred herds than in the case of grade animals, but no one contended that it was less than they could have got for those animals otherwise.

It is easy enough to bring someone in from the United States to put a valuation on the flock. We do not know who the men were. I do not know anything about Mr. Rock, although I understand he is very prominent and is well known in the United States, Great Britain and Canada for his success in the show ring and for the prices he has received for his animals. But I still say it is a tremendous price to pay for sheep.
If the price keeps going up the way it has over the last five years and the department makes it attractive to lose sheep infected with scrapie, they may find it more difficult to get rid of this disease. We had this experience with tuberculosis a few years ago, when people purposely had their cattle react because they could get a better price that way than any other. I suggest that the same thing is likely to happen in connection with scrapie, and it will be very hard for the department to trace these things. It has been suggested that there were some substitutions made in this flock before the date the animals were slaughtered and buried.
They had all been checked.

Can the minister stand up in this house and say that they were checked every time the departmental officials went out? Can he say that the ear tag numbers were taken on the first visit that was made to the flock, and that the ear tag numbers were checked with the ear tag numbers of the animals which were buried?

My hon. friend will
understand that I must depend upon my officials, and they tell me that they were all checked as soon as it had been established there was scrapie in the flock, and all those which had gone out before that were traced right through to their destination as far as that was possible in order to establish that there was no disease. Certainly there were no transfers after the scrapie was established. If sheep had gone to the United States with this disease or had carried it somewhere else, you had to go there and find it. They

did go there. All these examinations were made and as nearly as it can be said by anyone, I am quite prepared to stand here and say that we take the responsibility in the department for saying that no such thing did happen.

The minister is saying, then, that after the disease was diagnosed all ear tag numbers were taken, but I say to him that the disease was not diagnosed until many months and many years after it was suspected. What happened from the time it was suspected until the inspection was made? I suppose inspections were made to find out whether the disease had made any progress in the flock. Otherwise how would you know when to take out animals and send them to be slaughtered? If the flock was not inspected at intervals how would you know that there were any diseased animals? I understand the incubation period for this disease is two or three years, but very little is known about it.
The ear tag numbers may have been taken at the time of the first inspection of the flock, but what about sheep that had not yet been tagged? I admit that it would be an almost impossible job with 600 sheep. It would probably take days to check the ear tag numbers. I do not know how the inspections were made of this flock previous to the time the disease was suspected. This flock was brought to Toronto and shown at the winter fair just previous to the time the infected sheep was found, and the disease diagnosed as scrapie. So there are probably hundreds of sheep across the country now that have been in contact with sheep of this flock, and that is what makes it so alarming to the sheep breeders, especially in Ontario.
I do not know if all the sheep that were sold from this flock at the Royal winter fair last fall have been kept under surveillance and are being quarantined, whether any of them have been destroyed or what has happened to the sheep that came out of that flock. It should be known where every sheep is that was sold out of that flock in the last five years. I know how difficult it is for the officials, but I want to point out how serious it is. Perhaps the tags were removed. The minister knows as well as I do that things like that go on with registered livestock across this country, the switching of ear tags and so on. I am not suggesting it was done, but there are stories being circulated that some of these sheep that were supposed to have been destroyed and buried are still in the country. I think it is very important that we should know for sure whether it was done.

The men responsible for doing the job are sitting in front of me and

they say it was done. That is all I can tell you. Every type of sheep you mention has been traced right through and is still being checked, and no scrapie has developed as a result of any of them. The hon. member speaks of there being sometimes hundreds and sometimes many more, all of which gives the impression that probably the thing could not have been done. But I am told by the officials that it was done, and that every sheep that came down to the exhibition at Toronto and was sold and delivered has been traced right into the flocks where it is, and none of them has scrapie or any sign of it.
That was not my question.

As a veterinarian you can figure out all kinds of things, but there are as good veterinarians sitting here. They have gone all over it and checked it from every point of view, and they indicate to us that there is no possibility within reasonable limits of following these things up of scrapie having been carried from this flock elsewhere. The flock itself is all underground, buried.

There are two questions
the minister did not answer. One was, were the ear tag numbers taken on the first inspection of the flock? Right from the time the
disease was diagnosed the ear tag numbers were taken. I venture to say that my hon. friend does not get all the tags on all the nursery stock he has sold, as to whether there was disease in the roots and so on. It has been done just as carefully as it can be done. There is, of course, the question as to whether too much was paid. That is a legitimate question to raise. We do not think too much was paid. I have tried to keep strictly away from personalities in this discussion and I do not appreciate the minister's remarks regarding nursery stock, although perhaps it is true. His department inspects it. I do not think we have had anything go out that has not passed inspection.
The minister still has not answered my first question. Apparently the ear tag numbers were not taken. I have to assume that there were no ear tag numbers taken previous to the time the disease was actually diagnosed as scrapie. I am not saying this is

wrong and it should be done this way, but I am saying it is dangerous. What has been told might quite reasonably be true under those circumstances. I am not saying it is true, but the people who tell these stories know. That is all I am suggesting.
Bring them to the department.
It the ear tag numbers were not taken prior to the diagnosis, then there was plenty of time from the time the disease was established until the disease was diagnosed for a good many things to happen.

The ear tag numbers are all here, as my hon. friend knows. Those sheep were all registered, and the ear tag numbers were all known here, no matter when they were sold. The transfers are all registered. There is no great difficulty about tracing sheep that were there even ten years before the scrapie was there. But to say that every one of those sheep will have to be traced right back to the time Rock started to set up his flock, I do not think that is expected.
No one is suggesting that.

It might be said, "Perhaps you should know where all the sheep are that went out of that flock, say three months before the disease was in existence at all." That could probably be done and perhaps has been done. We can certainly And out where they went. Every flock that had any possibility of contamination through shipments of sheep from this flock has been checked. I know that rumours go around about things of that kind, but if one wants to follow up all the rumours there is no way of doing it. If any person mentions to any member of the house that he knows of these sheep, refer him to the department. It does not have to be a matter of publicity, but let him certainly come to the department and make known what he knows, and it will be checked right to the minute.

There is still another question the minister did not answer, and I think it is very important; that is, whether or not all the sheep sold from the flock within the past two or three years, say, which we assume is the incubation period for the disease-as far as we know it is two or three years-have been isolated. Are there any of those sheep across the country today that are not isolated from other sheep, or are they being used for breeding purposes anywhere?

There would be nothing gained by isolating them. They have been in

the flocks, and the flocks have been checked and they are still under observation.
The entire flock?
The entire flock where the animal is. That is, if Rock sold an animal into some particular flock, that flock is still under observation.

I am glad to hear that the whole flock is under observation. However, as this, we assume, is a hereditary disease, would it be good judgment or common sense to keep on using one of those rams, for instance, to breed ewes now after knowing it came from the Rock flock? Even though he were used for a year or only two months, would it be good common sense to keep on using him and have him breed several more ewes, knowing he is from the Rock flock?
My hon. friend is again assuming something with which I think no expert agrees. No one agrees it has been proven that the disease is hereditary.
Not proven, but it is certainly the assumption by some authorities.

It is not known that it is hereditary. All these matters that are being referred to are naturally under consideration in the observation that is being made of the flocks. The disease has been in existence, as I said a few minutes ago, in Britain for at least 200 years. They do not know the answers to these questions now, and I do not know that they will know them after we are all through with the observations that are being made, but the observations are being made, and in so far as can be found there is no trace of it elsewhere.
I suggest that it might be easier to get the answers now than it has been in the past 200 years.
It may take part of the next 100 years to get them through.

The minister did not answer my question, and I was quite serious about it.

I understand there was an attempt made to diagnose the disease, scrapie, and that brain samples have been taken of the condemned animals. Can he tell the committee if any findings have been made which would lead to establishing the cause of the disease and a method to control it? That is my first question. My second question has to do with certain statements made by other members of the committee in which they have tried to indicate that sheep from this flock have gone throughout the country and apparently also have gone, according to certain press reports, to many parts of the world.
I have a press report here indicating that a flock of 502 Canadian sheep have been flown to the Dominican Republic to improve flock blood lines in that Caribbean country. It indicates that many of the sheep came from the flock of P. J. Rock of Calgary. Incidentally, the date of the press report is March 17, approximately the same date as the discussion that took place in the house with respect to the action taken by the government to destroy many of the sheep in Mr. Rock's flock. I would ask the minister if he has any report to make on the sheep that have been shipped to the Dominican Republic. With respect to the destruction of the condemned animals on Mr. Rock's farm, can the minister tell the committee whether the complete flock was destroyed? It would seem to me that the compensation is entirely out of line with what one might call simple justice.
I am a purebred breeder myself, and I think the minister will agree with the statement when I say that you cannot take the top sale price figure as representing a fair price for your complete herd. Often purebred breeders in the cattle business as well as those in sheep and other livestock businesses get a fairly good price at public auction, but you cannot say that would be a fair price for a complete herd of cattle or a complete flock of sheep. I think the price of approximately $670 per sheep is completely out of line-

To begin with, and to follow up the simile used at the commencement of my hon. friend's remarks, I might say that I am not one of those animals which goes around with wool in its teeth. In any case, the answer has already been given to the question. I read it. Progress on this type of project is invariably slow, for the first thing that must be done is a thorough microbiological examination of all brains and spinal cords, and this work is now being done. A search is also under way for the causative agent in the spleens, livers and kidneys, but no results are yet available from this work.
In other words we have not been able to discover, any more than they have in Britain or elsewhere up to now, just what is the cause of the disease. I think that answers the question which was in the hon. member's mind when he wanted to know if the cause had been traced. It also answers the suggestion that the disease is hereditary. As to the price, I quite admit that I do not know very much about the price of sheep; but my hon. friend who lives near Mr. Rock says he did sell sheep for as much as $1,000. 20.	Administration of Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and Meat and Canned Foods Act, $5,698,838.

What information can the minister give us relative to the inoculation of cattle leaving Winnipeg yards for haemorrhagic septicemia? What has been the result? Has it been good? Have you had to pay much compensation for animals that have died as a result of that disease?

For some years the department provided shipping fever anti-serum free to stockyards where feeder cattle were being assembled for shipment. A few years ago some doubt arose as to the actual efficiency of this anti-serum in preventing shipping fever, and extensive field tests were conducted by the department in the fall of 1954. These established that the anti-serum had in fact very limited beneficial effect in controlling shipping fever and the free distribution of that product was discontinued by the department last year.
The work which has been done on the matter indicates that other organisms are involved in the condition known as shipping fever, and that the most feasible control probably would be in the bacterin containing these various organisms. Various types of bacterin for this purpose were prepared last year by the department's animal pathology division and subjected to trials with experimental lots of animals at the department's own station. As a result of this one product was determined to have the most beneficial value, and it is proposed to use this on field trials during the coming fall.
The survey was commenced in October, 1954, and completed in December, 1954. During this period 2,093 animals were treated with bacterin and 4,062 treated with serum. Approximately 3,255 animals were identified as control animals, receiving neither serum nor bacterin. Bacterin was administered on the ranch, 10 days to six weeks in advance of the sales date, and serum at the shipping point, one to four days before shipment.
Immediately prior to treatment, blood samples were collected from approximately 10 per cent of the three groups. Blood tested animals were identified and a second sample collected after arrival on the purchasers' premises.
The purpose of blood tests was to measure by means of the complement fixation test any change in antibody level between the time of shipping in the west and arrival at destination in the east.
On arrival at destination in eastern Canada the animals were visited on the purchasers' premises at least twice, and where sick animals were encountered, departmental veterinarians provided treatment. Suitable specimens from animals which died were forwarded to the laboratory in Hull for study and, in particular, to determine the type or types of bacteria responsible for the disease.
Of the 9,410 animals shipped, 266 or 6-5 per cent of the 4,062 serum-treated animals were sick on arrival; 49 or 2-3 per cent of the 2,093 bacterin-treated animals were sick on arrival; and 177 or 5-4 per cent of the

3,255 untreated animals were sick on arrival. The mortality in these groups was 35 (0-86 per cent) in the serum group; 10 (0-47 per cent) in the bacterin group; and 30 (0-92 per cent) in the control group. This is shown in Table 1.

I wonder if the minister could give us some idea of the success of our testing for T.B. reactors in cattle, and the progress of the testing throughout the different districts?
I understand the question is as to the percentage, after they have been tested?
I should like to know also if it looks as though the situation is improving down through the years?

Oh, yes, there is no question about that. This concerns the program of tuberculine testing and restricted area retesting. I have here the estimated number of cattle to be retested, the estimated percentage of tuberculosis and the estimated amount required for the payment of compensation for reactors slaughtered. This is for the year 1956-57, and it is based on our experience, of course. The number tested right across Canada for 1949-50 was 2,089,000. The number of reactors was 30,521. The compensation paid was $1,261,771.60. If you remember, in 1949-50 it was 2,098,000 and in 1954-55 it was 2,079,000 that were tested. In 1949-50 there were 30,521 reactors and in 1954-55 there were 3,900, just a little more than one-tenth.
You have not the percentage there, I take it.

You would find there were not more than one-ninth as many reactors last year as there were in 1949-50, and that is a six-year period. The amount paid this year will be $192,665 as against $1,261,000 before.

The hon. member for Queens is unavoidably absent on committee work and I know he would like a question asked regarding a case of lungworm that has been found, or at least suspected, in Prince Edward Island. Apparently this is the only case of lungworm that has ever been diagnosed as such. Apparently the farm now occupied by this farmer was once either a substation or a farm used for experimental purposes in some way. Now, as this lungworm is apparently found solely within the animal-the egg is picked up off the ground and passes its entire life cycle in the animal; there is no intermediary host-it is just possible, although I am not saying it is true, that these eggs might have been lying there for

some years from experimental work that was being carried on at the farm previously.
I think, although there has never been compensation paid for this, something should be done. Probably the cattle will take a long time to die. If they are not all slaughtered right now, they are in such poor condition when they do die that they are not worth anything for beef. It is a very debilitating disease, and they do lose a tremendous amount of weight. As this is the only case known in Canada, I think it would be only fair that this particular chap should receive compensation. Probably he has not been on the farm too long and has not too good a start, so probably could not afford to be put on the expense of losing his entire herd. Perhaps there is someway by which compensation could be paid and something learned from a study of the carcasses which was not known before. If they were slaughtered they might be worth something for experimental purposes.

The only thing I can say is that the existence of the disease, if you could call it that, has been reported to the department and investigations have been started. We have not yet any report on it. If it has not already been done I would suggest to the hon. member that he give us all the particulars of the case about which he is speaking. Then we could keep track of it and if there is any necessity for doing anything we could do it.
I think the minister misunderstood me. The hon. member for Queens has spoken to me on this and he is unavoidably absent. I was mentioning it on his behalf.
You have the hon. member send us particulars.
I think he was talking to the department, and presumably that is why the investigation is going ahead.

It is going ahead. On the question of whether the individual is to be paid compensation, I presume that particular disease is not named amongst those for which we do pay compensation, but that does not prevent something being done.
It does not prevent an order in council being passed. I suggest that has been done in other cases and this is a case in which that might be done.

To provide for grants to fairs and exhibitions in accordance with regulations of the governor in council: for payments pursuant to agreements in force on March 31, 1956, with exhibition associations covering the construction of buildings and other major undertakings; and for a grant of $50,000 to the royal agricultural winter fair, Toronto, and freight assistance on livestock shipments for exhibition thereat, $926,500.

In Medicine Hat, as you know, we have stampede exhibitions every year which last for three days. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture knows more about that than I do, but we have never received a grant from the federal government or the provincial government. What I am wondering is how to go about getting a grant for a three-day stampede and exhibition, such as we have.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member knows that we make grants to B fairs and A fairs, and they must qualify under the regulations to be designated as a B fair before they are entitled to any grant from here. The fairs below that category do have grants from provincial governments at different rates in the different provinces, but we establish the claim entirely on the basis as to whether they have paid out $5,000 over a period of years for an A fair and $3,000 for a B fair. If Medicine Hat has had a fair for three years and it has paid out $3,000 or more in prizes, then they have every right to apply here for a grant. The fact that they have not had one either indicates that they have not been paying out that much or they have not made application for it. There may be some other

Mr. Chairman, I am looking for information. When I read the Medicine Hat News I find there are so many conflicting statements that I just wonder where they come from. One party says that the federal government will not do anything and another one says, yes, they will if you go about it the right way. I am looking for information and I must thank the minister for the information he has given me.
I notice some of these grants are for special fairs. What is included in that? There are class A fairs and class B fairs and then special fairs.

We have an arrangement that started with New Brunswick, but we have it now with Newfoundland also; just the two, Newfoundland and New Brunswick, under which we make payments and they make payments. It is a little different from the other provinces.

It is the policy of the Department of Agriculture to pay fairly substantial grants to fairs that qualify as class A and class B. I am suggesting that possibly the class C fair should receive a grant for capital expenditures. I think that with respect to class A and class B fairs the department pays 25 per cent of the permanent capital expenditures. I would suggest that class C fairs could be treated along similar lines and be given a percentage of the capital expenditures they make at those fairs.

As I said a moment ago, class C fairs are considered to be fairs that are assisted by the provinces. I think during the relief period we did follow the plan which is now suggested and we did make grants to fairs in the C category for putting up certain buildings for the showing of their livestock and that kind of thing. But, as is known by hon. members, when the war started we stopped all those grants, and when we started them up again after the war and after the period in which relief was given we again confined them to the A and B fairs. We expect that the provinces are probably giving assistance to the others.

Under item 23 freight assistance is paid on livestock shipments for exhibition at the Royal agricultural winter fair at Toronto. I realize this is not a very large item when compared With many other items in the estimates. Can the minister tell us what formula is used in granting this assistance?

Well, the general policy is that the province pays the freight assistance on the livestock that is coming to the exhibition in all the provinces with the exception of Ontario. Nothing is paid there because it is close to the fair, I presume; at least, nothing is paid by the federal government. When we are billed for it we pay 75 per cent of the freight that has been paid by the provinces.
In every province with the exception of Ontario?
Excepting Ontario.

Is the

Taking the index of fertilizer prices for 1939 as 100-2, they advanced to 181-2 in 1955 and in January, 1956, they were 181-1. Mr. Chairman, I have

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the committee wish to take item 601 with item 27?
No, Mr. Chairman.

I have one question I should like to ask on item 27. There has been a good deal of discussion lately in Medicine Hat, as the minister knows, about cold storage plants. We realize that in southern Alberta we can raise the best corn of any part of Canada. Perhaps we have more dry weather and more sunshine. However, by the time it leaves the field and gets to the city of Edmonton or the city of Calgary it is a little wetter, one might say. There have been discussions in Medicine Hat regarding the building of a cold storage plant.
I have noticed that other cities have had assistance from the government in that regard. I am wondering whether the city of Medicine Hat or the people of Medicine Hat can get assistance to build a cold storage plant so we can process our corn, put it in sacks and deliver it to many points, not only to Edmonton and Calgary but to Winnipeg, for instance, where they never have good corn. Medicine Hat is the one place where we raise good corn, and I think we should know how to go about building a cold storage plant so we can ship our corn out of Medicine Hat in first class condition.

The hon. member for Medicine Hat asked how people go about getting grants for cold storage plants. The act provides that if the conditions are met as set out in the act, the government pays a subsidy of 33| per cent of the cost. They pay it all in the year when the plant is constructed. That requires, of course, that somebody else pay the other two-thirds, and that somebody else may be a co-operative or an individual concern that undertakes to put in cold storage. That assistance has been given now over quite a few years and it is available to Medicine Hat in common with other places.
I realize that that assistance is available, and I am very glad to have the minister's answer so we shall know just what to expect from the government.

This item refers to cold storage plants. I should like to ask the minister whether under this item might be taken up the matter of frozen food plants. They are called by a different name, nevertheless they are for the processing of agricultural products in order to keep them in a

fresh state for the market. In our province there is at least one firm that is considering seriously, and in fact is going ahead with such a plant. 1 know that the firm has been to Ottawa and discussed this with the departmental officials. Does that come under this item, and is there a possibility of their getting assistance from the department under these grants?

I believe there is an application from Saint John, New Brunswick, for cold storage of some type. There has been some question raised as to whether it conforms in all particulars with our legislation. I am not in a position to say whether or not that is the case; but freezer plants of a type come under the act; that is, the type of plant that puts in lockers. If it is a cooperative it comes under the act; if it is not a co-operative, it does not.
Then there is another type of freezing plant which has no lockers. The five plants that are spoken of in the west are of a new type of freezer different from what we have had, except for one plant at Vancouver. There are some others contemplated elsewhere. I think it depends somewhat on what my hon. friend means by freezer plants; but they have made application and the matter is being considered.

The minister speaks of a locker plant. We have a locker plant. That locker plant is privately owned, but it does not prepare foods like a frozen food plant. Up to the present time we have been importing into this country from the United States large amounts of frozen foods, even into our own province; strawberries, peas, beans, rhubarb and all sorts of things like that. I think there is room for the development of what we refer to as a frozen food products plant. I gather from what the minister has said that if it is a co-operative arrangement it comes within the act, but if it is not a co-operative arrangement it does not come within the act. Am I right?

You are right about the locker plants. If the locker plant is owned by a local butcher, for example, as it is in my own town in the west, he does not get a subsidy under this act; but if the people, either in the town or in the country round about, organize themselves into a co-operative and have a freezer plant, they do get 33J per cent assistance.
On the other type of plant, the condition is that the plant must be open to the public. If an individual goes into the business of freezing food products, in the sense of taking them in, freezing them and selling them to the public, I doubt very much whether he comes under the act; but if a person simply
Supply-Agriculture
has a freezer plant and allows the general public to bring products in to be frozen, and then the people sell them, I do not think there is much question about that. Nevertheless I would want to have the case referred to the justice department before saying definitely that it could meet the conditions under the act.

In the vicinity where I live and for miles around we grow fine vegetables, but we can grow a great many more than we can consume. If I understood the minister, the plant would have to be one that would be open for freezing and processing and I as a farmer could take vegetables and have them frozen and processed but it would be up to me to sell them. Is that what the minister means; or would it be the case that the plant would purchase the vegetables from the farmer, freeze them and then ship them to other parts of the province or outside the province? In other words it would become a local business. If they could get assistance under these arrangements, then what is the difference between a co-operative building a plant and 15 farmers or 15 businessmen getting together and building a plant? In the second place, if they can come under the provision, will they get assistance not only in the building of the plant but in the furnishing of the machinery and equipment?

It is very difficult to answer a question of that kind without knowing all the particulars in connection with it. Those are just the things that we are becoming acquainted with in connection with the application that has been made. In general terms the position is that if a man puts up a plant and then says that all his space is for rent; then somebody else buys the commodities from the farmers in the neighbourhood, puts them in there and then takes them out and sells them, and I think that is pretty generally done, we have paid the 33J per cent. But if the individual who owns the plant goes right into the business himself and utilizes all the space, and there is no space for the general public at all, then I have no doubt about that case either. He does not come under the act.
There may be some place in between where the line would have to be drawn in a legal sense, but I should not like to try to define it here. There proper procedure is the one they are following of writing us, as they did. They will get a reply and we will have adjustments of ideas, because there has to be a certain percentage of the plant utilized for certain purposes. If a man has constructed a building and most of the space in it is occupied with something else, he would have difficulty in coming under the act.

Supply-Agriculture

I think this application came from an area quite near my home, and I know such a plant would be of great advantage to many of the farmers there who have been in trouble over potatoes. If we could get them to change to mixed farming, garden farming and one thing and another it might be of great benefit. I hope the minister and the department will give as generous construction to the act and assistance to these people as they possibly can.

Yes, that will be met. We have already had communications, but up to now they have not actually made an application. They are asking for the kind of information the hon. member is seeking. They will get it, and if they submit an application it will be considered.
Would the grant be available to a co-operative to buy a plant that is already in existence?

No, the regulation is quite definite on that point. If they even proceed to build a plant before they have been authorized by us to go ahead with it we do not pay. They must present their case and have it considered before they have a plant at all. Not even the buying of the property is consented to under the act.

The minister did not get my point. I know of a case of locker facilities already in existence where the owner is gradually going bankrupt. If a co-operative in the district wanted to purchase that locker plant could they get a grant?
They had better get in touch with us before they do. If they define the case as it is they will probably get word back indicating that they can or cannot.

I noted carefully the last few words of the minister, and I have had a problem placed before me by the Shuswap Okanagan dairy industries co-operative association of Vernon. Last year they made an application to the department for the subsidy in connection with the building of cold storage facilities for a branch which they were opening in Kamloops. Technical difficulties arose, and I must admit that the dairy did go ahead before final approval was given. Apparently the plant meets all the specifications of the department, and if it had not been for this technicality they would have been eligible for the subsidy.
However, when I took up the matter the other day I was advised that it might be reconsidered, but that since the main and supplementary estimates had already been prepared it was doubtful if anything could be done this year. I must say I was rather surprised when I looked at the top of page

118 to see an amount of $6,500 provided in this year's estimates with this designation: "Kamloops, Shuswap Okanagan dairy industries co-operative association." These two facts do not jibe, and possibly the minister could give us an explanation at this time.

The only explanation I can give is that when I was in that area, I think it was last fall, I had the pleasure of visiting the plant along with those who are on the board. There are some misunderstandings that have not been cleared up and unless they are cleared satisfactorily there will not be a grant, but I am not prepared to say at this moment whether there will or will not be a grant.

Before the item carries may I say that the comments of some hon. members are very reminiscent of problems that some of us have had in dealing with this item in the past. I was a little surprised to hear the minister say that the whole 33J per cent is paid in one payment. I think the regulation in that respect must have been changed-
That is right; two years ago.

-because as I recall it was paid in three annual instalments and that used to provoke some difficulty. The minister also spoke of co-operatives as if this grant was only payable to co-operatives, but I think it is also payable to privately owned plants provided they make provision for public use of the cold storage facilities.
Yes. It is only in the case of locker plants that we only pay to co-operatives.

I want to add one thing
further. I hope the minister and his departmental officials will give pretty careful consideration to the regulations. I have had quite a bit of experience with them. I certainly want to congratulate the department and the officers generally on the way in which they have administered this rather difficult problem, because I think every hon. member has pressure brought to bear on him with regard to installing a cold storage plant in an inadequate building. It seems to be felt that if the member has sufficient political pull he will be able to get a subsidy. This has created difficulties, but I think that on the whole the department has administered the plan very well.
In fact, I think it is perhaps a little bit too strict, and I want to give one illustration. I have in mind a cold storage plant in Nova Scotia owned by the United Fruit Company which met the specifications of the department. It was one on which a subsidy had been paid and it was as modem as most cold

storage plants in Canada. The company-proposed to put in a vegetable cold storage branch in connection with the fruit. There was to be separate construction. It was to be a part of the same building but an addition to it. I am sure that everything would have been of the most modern construction, that the most modern machinery would have been installed and all the rest of it. Yet because of some technical interpretation of the regulation-and I am not quarrelling with the administration, because I think it was interpreted fairly although strictly by the officials -that cold storage grant was refused on account of the particular wording of the regulation. I can assume also that in the relatively near future the minister will receive some requests.
I am looking for an item which is not here and which I cannot find in the supplementary estimates, but I will ask him about that matter later. For instance, he will be interested to know that the new apple marketing organization in the valley is meeting today for the first time. As to the possibilities of cold storage developments there, for instance I can imagine gas storage, perhaps in smaller units, being installed within the relatively near future. That development again is going to raise the question of installation in existing structures rather than perhaps the construction of entirely new ones.
I hope the minister will ask his officials responsible for this matter to consider these regulations very carefully so that the spirit will be observed as well as, we hope, the letter. I suggest that when adequate modern cold storage facilities are brought into being they be encouraged in every way possible rather than be perhaps denied encouragement because of a technical or I will say a strict interpretation of what is possibly an overly strict regulation.
We have paid subsidies on two plants-one in Quebec and one in Ontario-that have this gas system of cold storage.

Item agreed to.
Marketing service-
28.	Agricultural economics, $637,362.

Can the minister tell me whether the economics branch here in the dominion department is co-operating with the department of economics at the provincial level with regard to these booklets that the department of economics at Guelph is putting out to help farmers in keeping their books and preparing their income tax returns? Is there any liaison between the two departments or is it made general? Are the
Supply-Agriculture
people across Canada getting the benefit of the booklet the Ontario people have, or is it just in Ontario?
Yes, we have had co-operative studies between our officials and the Ontario officials in preparing that booklet.
Is it being printed by the dominion department and made available to farmers across Canada, or is it just made available in Ontario?

My information is that it is one of the publications of the province, that it is being printed by them. However, I assume that if we were going to put it in any of the other provinces probably we would have to have understandings with the provincial departments there as well.

I suggest to the minister that it is a very good book and that it is very helpful to farmers in keeping their books and in making their income tax returns. I think it would be a good suggestion if the minister would look into the matter further and find out whether the other provincial governments would not co-operate with this department and see that it is made available to other farmers across the dominion.

Item agreed to.
Marketing service-
29.	Dairy products, $798,723.

There has been a considerable amount of controversy lately about cheese production in that we do not know for sure how much cheese there is going to be for export. The home consumption has gone up quite a bit. I maintain that production is not keeping pace with the increasing domestic demand for cheese. I wonder what the department is doing to meet the situation.
As the minister knows, cheese is one of the products for which, in most years at least, we have been able to get a premium on the United Kingdom market. I think the situation now is that we could probably demand a premium of 2 cents or 3 cents in the United Kingdom market for cheese if we had it to export at this time. I wonder whether the minister can give us any information as to what is being done to aid the cheese producers to build up again this export market in the United Kingdom?

To begin with, we have an agreement with the Ontario cheese producers. They have a new name. They changed their name last week, I think it was. In any event, the hon. member knows whom I mean. I refer to the co-operative cheese producers in Ontario. We have an agreement with them under which we guarantee them at the bank for 22-5 cents a pound or

I want to say just a word about selling cheese in Canada. I know my wife complains that when she goes into these big super markets right here in Ottawa, about half the time she cannot get any good, plain, ordinary Canadian cheese. They have nothing but this Kraft stuff and other substitutes.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No. I rather hesitate to go along with the minister's idea that all the cheese that is produced here in Canada could be sold here. It is working to that end, I will agree. I will say this for the chain stores; they have done a remarkable job of merchandising cheese. Why? Because they put it up in attractive packages that people like. They like to see what they are getting. The chain stores have done a remarkable job in increasing the consumption of cheese. It is true that much of it is soft cheese or processed cheese but there is a good deal of cheddar, both white and coloured.
I think it is a mistake to depend entirely on the domestic market. Even if we reduce the consumption in the domestic market and hold the product off the domestic market, I think the United Kingdom market should be maintained if that is at all possible. As I say-and I think I am correct in saying it -at the present time the United Kingdom is paying for Canadian cheese a premium of at least 2 cents over some of the other cheese. I think they are quite willing to pay it, at least I understand they are, for Canadian cheese. I believe that consideration is sufficient to warrant a little increase in the production of cheese, with enough set aside of our Canadian production, to maintain at least a quota in the United Kingdom market.

I do not know that this is the time to discuss that particular point. However, I would point out that the British have always paid a premium for our cheese over and above New Zealand cheese, which is the big source of the supply that comes into the country. New Zealand sells to Britain far more than we sell, and has been doing so ever since the first war. During that time Britain gave us a premium of up to 3 cents over New Zealand cheese, but at the present time all Britain is buying from us is what they must have to serve a certain part of the trade.
Under that condition, up to this year they were buying our cheese from the board at 2 cents less than cheese was being sold in Ontario. I am not saying we were very enthusiastic about that, any more than some people were enthusiastic about our selling butter cheaper in some places. Nevertheless, under the circumstances under which they were doing that, probably it was the proper thing. It is their business.
What I mean by saying it can be sold in Canada is that we have great difficulty after we get west of Winnipeg in getting cheddar cheese. My friend says there is difficulty in getting it in Ottawa. If there is difficulty in getting it in Ottawa I would say there is 10 times as much difficulty in getting it after you get west of Winnipeg. We know from experience that the cheese that is now made can be sold there at a higher price than you have been selling it to Britain. I am not saying you should not sell any to Britain. They are selling it, and they are doing so in order to try to stay in that market. It is their business and they make their own decisions about it.
There is one other thing I should have said when I was speaking before. We, of course, pay a premium of 2 cents on 94 score cheese and we pay a premium of 1 cent on

93 score cheese. This is paid in addition to the other assistance which we give in connection with cheese.

I was tempted by the remark of my hon. friend from Vancouver South to ask the minister when cheese is not cheese. What I mean is, is there any regulation or any pure food law which would compel people putting up these packaged cheeses to state upon the package the contents? I know that a great many people who buy these packaged cheeses, so-called, are under the impression that they are buying cheese. Actually they are not buying it. My friend calls it a substitute, but I would call it a mixture of this and that. A great many people in the west are not too familiar with what good cheese is. They are under the impression that because they have these dairy factories in the east, they are getting good cheese when they buy that stuff.

I do not want to be critical of Kraft, for example, who put up a great deal of this cheese. Two years ago we had a discussion along this line and I made the rather definite statement that you could not buy cheddar cheese in the west. One check we made revealed that there was only one store in the west that had good cheddar cheese, and that was in Calgary. It was a special cheese store. Apparently the Kraft people paid more attention to the remark than anybody else, and since that time they have begun to cut up these big cheeses into half pound packages, and wrap them properly, and they have been selling them on the prairies at a very good price. I think it costs about 76 cents a pound when it gets out there in that form, so no one is losing any money on that particular sale.
The point I want to make is that while we were trying to encourage some people to become interested in selling this cheese out there by telling them where there was a market in which they could sell it, the Kraft people listened to us more than the people to whom we were trying to talk. They went out there and sold it, and you can get good cheddar cheese in the stores now.

I think there is a point that the people learn to eat cheese by eating cheese. So long as they eat some of the stuff they are eating at the moment I do not think they will ever learn what good cheese is. Therefore there will never be a demand created for good cheese. I have not mentioned any manufacturer's name, but I do not believe the minister has quite answered my question.
The point I want to get at is this. Is there a regulation or law which prohibits these

people from selling anything as cheese which is not, in fact, cheese undiluted; that is the point.

Yes, there are composition standards. Of course when you take what is generally known as Kraft it has been specially prepared, and is sold as that .The dealer does not attempt to sell it as anything but what it is, but it is not what we generally call cheddar cheese.

Does the Kraft company, which has probably imported more cheese into this country than anybody else, sell that cheese as New Zealand cheese or is it mixed up with Ontario cheese and sold as Canadian cheese?

Well, most of it is brought in for processing. Some of it is sold directly on the market, depending on who brings it in. If the Kraft people bring it in, they use it for making up this special Kraft cheese. It is a processed cheese. It may have some Canadian cheese in it, but there is more moisture in it than is in the ordinary cheese.

I do not think that is right.
I do not think they should be allowed to bring in New Zealand cheese and mix it with our good cheese and sell it at a high price, taking a huge profit. That is what it amounts to, so far as I can see.
In so far as this processed cheese is concerned, I presume the regulations would be somewhat similar to the butter regulations. Is there any moisture content that the cheese has to contain?
Yes, both moisture and salt.
In cheese?
There is a salt regulation for cheese, too.
Is there a moisture regulation?
There is a regulation for moisture and salt.
Does the soft cheese have to conform to a standard? How about cheese spreads; is there any standard for them?
There is a standard for it.

What about ice cream? As we all know, there is a good deal of what is sometimes called frozen custard or of ice cream sold under various names. What is the standard of butter fat content for that soft ice cream, if it is properly called soft ice cream? Is it within the law to call it soft ice cream of must it be called some other name? What are the regulations under which that is sold in comparison with real ice cream?

Supply-Agriculture

The ice cream regulations are to the effect that ice cream shall contain not less than 10 per cent by weight of milk fat; not less than 36 per cent by weight of food solids; not less than 1-8/10 pounds of food solids per gallon, of which more than 50/100ths of a pound shall be milk and not more than J of 1 per cent by weight of stabilizer, and so on. The regulations are all set out.
It is within the law, then, to call this soft product, whatever it is, soft ice cream?
So far as the content of it is concerned, it is within the law. It is just not frozen as solidly as the other.
Is it correct to say that it cannot be frozen hard? Does it contain too much moisture, and if it were frozen hard the crystals would show up?
My experience has been that the ice cream that cannot be frozen hard is nearly all cream. We make it at home sometimes, but you cannot buy it in the stores.

Their duty is to enforce the stockyard and livestock regulations under the Livestock and Livestock Products Act at the different stockyards where they are in charge.
I take it that it is more of an inspection job than anything else, to see that the act is followed. Is that the idea?

34. Marketing of agricultural products, including temporary appointments that may be required to be made notwithstanding the Civil Service Act, the amount available for such appointments not to exceed $6,000, $100,000.

Just what is included in this item? It says, "marketing of agricultural products". We have various groups for livestock, poultry and cheese, and we have had everything else. I was wondering just what is included in the marketing of products. In the breakdown there is an item for marketing projects, about $55,000. I should like the minister to give us a word of explanation with respect to that.
I also see there is a provision here that has to do with appointments notwithstanding the

Civil Service Act. The amount available for such purpose is not to exceed $6,000. That looks almost like a casual appointment. In any event I am wondering just what is proposed, because when I turn to the breakdown I find there is a lot of money available for casual employment. I have something else to say about that in a minute, but I should like to get from the minister a picture of just what is involved in the item.

Mr. Chairman, when I first came to the department 20 years ago there was not any marketing service in the department. When we made the classification which I indicated earlier, when we were talking about splitting it up again, we brought in those five branches, marketing being one of them, and we set up certain amounts for the promotion of the marketing of farm products. In more recent days-I think it actually came up during the war and has been continued since-we asked to have an amount put in for advertising farm products. One of the uses that we did make of it was putting those advertisements out all over the country before we started the present butter program. "Butter is better" is one advertisement that we put all over the place, and it did increase the sale of butter. Anything that is undertaken that way we finance out of this fund. If we were to start out, for example, to promote the sale of more cheese or the eating of more apples the money would come out of this fund.
Then at that time we had in mind setting up a plan under which we might carry on greater operations than this amount of money would provide for, and we put in this one salary under the condition that we could not pay a man any more than $6,000. As a matter of fact we have not paid him up to date; we have been using the money for advertising purposes.

What is proposed, Mr. Chairman? I understand advertising. There is a provision of $35,000 in the breakdown for advertising. Then we have $52,300 for marketing projects. Just what is involved in the term, and what is done under those marketing projects?
Well, it is utilized for the study of marketing problems such as grading bacon, grading butter, grading cheese or products of that kind.
Would that not come under the vote of the department? The minister has separate funds for livestock-

It could, but the hon. member will note that this is something that goes on. These marketing projects are, for example, something that we start up and

carry on for two or three months or for six months, and for that reason we do not think we should set up a civil service appointment in order to cover that particular work. We get some person appointed. He may be a provincial man or he may be a man engaged in the dairy industry somewhere who can do this job for us and we pay him up to $6,000. We cannot pay him any more on these projects that the hon. member speaks of. He may be examining into one of these projects, is our bacon properly graded, is our butter properly graded, and so on? We have him check on that and report to us.
Can the minister give us an example of the project that he proposes to carry out under this $6,000 vote?

The one that is on at present is in connection with the project for bacon that I have just spoken of. We have a project on now in Montreal studying the grading of bacon to determine whether or not it is being done in the proper way and whether the public are being sold what they think they are getting. Take the matter that we discussed in the house about five years ago about putting coloured paper on bacon, and so on. These are the kinds of things that are investigated under these projects.

I can quite realize the importance of this. I shall draw the minister's attention to a marketing project to which I wish he would give some special attention in the immediate future, in co-operation with the Department of Trade and Commerce. He will know that Great Britain has now released sterling exchange, or it is released so far as the British West Indies are concerned. There is a potential market there for the sale of Nova Scotia apples at a relatively profitable price. Last year as well there was a market there, but owing to the fact there was not sufficient cold storage space available I know of one firm which lost a market for 4,000 boxes of apples at a relatively high price.
I realize that the Department of Agriculture does not control transport, but in view of the sudden announcement of the relaxation of restrictions on sterling I can pretty well envisage what is going to happen in the next few months with respect to that market. I do think there should be the closest co-operation between the Department of Agriculture marketing branch and the Department of Transport to find out what cold
Supply-Agriculture
storage space is going to be available in Canadian National Steamships-and there will not be enough-and also to see if arrangements can be made with ships plying between Montreal and the Caribbean that have cold storage space that could, of course, stop at Halifax or Saint John to pick up those apples which, for the first time since before the war at any rate, will have access without any restrictions on exchange to not an extensive market but to a reasonably profitable one and one which is highly desirable to foster in every way possible.
Will the minister mark that down as the No. 1 marketing project? If he does, I shall vote unanimously and enthusiastically for the passing of this particular item.
I shall consider it.

I notice that in the year 1954-55, $10,336 was spent under this item. For the year 1955-56 the actual expenditure to December 1, 1955, was $7,431 and the estimated balance for the year, $16,469. I suggest to the minister that the marketing service is one of the most important branches in this whole Dominion of Canada so far as agriculture is concerned. I suggest that very seriously, because marketing is the most important segment of the agricultural problem right now.
I am not criticizing in any way the amount of money that is spent, either in a special project or in any other project, if it is going to do some good in the marketing of agricultural products, but I wonder how the item of $100,000 is arrived at when last year's figure was only $23,900? I suggest the minister must have something in view. Since it is six o'clock perhaps I could ask him to bring in the program the next time the estimates are up and give us some of the projects that he is planning to do this year over and above those that were done last year.
